### §. I.

That human understanding, even in merely natural matters, is afflicted by countless infirmities <term>Kranckheiten; literally "diseases," used here to describe intellectual flaws or limitations</term>, is such an incontrovertibly manifest truth that even the pagan philosophers <note>original: "heydnischen Weltweisen"</note> themselves never doubted it. And sorrowful experience confirms daily that our knowledge <term>Erkänntniß; the capacity for cognition or awareness</term> is confined within all too narrow bounds—so much so, that we are often most subject to errors when we imagine ourselves to have seen into the truth of matters most precisely. Indeed, we mostly possess only an obscure and indistinct concept of those things which our pride <note>original: "Hochmuth"—referring here to intellectual arrogance or overconfidence in one's own reasoning.</note> would persuade us we understand quite clearly.

In particular, we may rightly count those troublesome prejudices <term>Vorurtheile; preconceived notions that cloud judgment before evidence is weighed</term> among these dangerous infirmities, and justly grant them the primary place. One need only take as an example several philosophers from different sects <note>original: "Secten"—referring to different schools of philosophical thought (e.g., Aristotelians, Cartesians).</note>, and it will be easy to perceive that each one judges the most important matters not so much according to their true nature, but rather according to the preconceived opinions of those se-

What, indeed, induces a so-called **Episcopalian** in England to believe that in the early Church all **rites** <term>ritus; ceremonial practices or religious customs</term> and customs were practiced that are still observed among them to this day? Nothing other than the ill-founded **prejudice** <term>Vorurtheil; a preconceived opinion not based on reason or actual evidence</term> that the Church to which he belongs deserves to be called the one most similar to the Apostles. I could elaborate on this at greater length, if my intention were not rather directed toward dealing with far more disadvantageous and harmful prejudices.

The former [the children of God] strive with every conceivable zeal to be freed from them more and more; the latter, on the other hand, indulge in them with total pleasure. The former recognize their weakness; the latter view their weakness as highly valuable virtues. The former pray and beseech the **Lord** in humility for the forgiveness of their errors; the latter do not even want to admit that they are afflicted by them. To the former, God does not count these errors toward their **perdition**; for the latter, however, they result in inevitable eternal harm.

# II. Prejudice.
## One cannot have a correct concept of GOD.

->§. 5.<-

There are indeed still people, even among the most wicked, who do not exactly doubt the existence and truth of the divine Being. Nonetheless, they do not wish to take the trouble to properly learn about this Creator of theirs according to His nature, will, and benefits. They are like flowing water, which moves further and further away from its source. They act like the unreasoning swine, which indeed devour the acorns under the trees in the forest with great appetite, but do not easily raise their eyes <note>The author uses a common moral trope: animals enjoy the fruits of nature without looking up to acknowledge the source, much like ungrateful humans.</note>

### §. 4.

Well then, let us see if there is no means available to clear this prejudice out of the way. **God** has indeed placed two great and very important books before the eyes of man. <note>The "Two Books" is a classic theological concept: the Book of Nature (the physical world) and the Book of Scripture (the Bible).</note> Study diligently within them, and you will obtain a correct concept of your Creator. Consider, after all, that mere matter is dead in itself and can in no way possess movement from its own nature. But you see that the growth of all bodies consists of movement. Why then will you not believe that your Creator is a spirit and has no body? ## III. Prejudice.
### A precise knowledge of **GOD** is not necessary for the attainment of salvation <note>original: "Seligkeit"; refers to the state of eternal bliss or being saved in a religious sense.</note>.

Whereby it then happens that the **LORD** must complain about them: *Your thoughts are not my thoughts*, Isaiah 55, 8. You, as an unreasoning creature, venture to criticize what your all-wise Creator has ordained and prescribed for you to do. 

Consider how intolerable your audacity is. Could you possibly justify the conduct of one who is overwhelmed with new benefits every day, yet would not want to learn to recognize the benefactor himself? You will undoubtedly have to agree with me that such a person has the highest need to concern themselves with an accurate knowledge of their benefactor, so that they might not remain lacking in the due gratitude for His extraordinary goodness. And behold, you can count more divine blessings than there are moments in your life. How then will you show your gratitude if you do not even recognize the exceedingly benevolent GOD?

->One can be saved in one religion just as well as in another.<-

If, however, it is said elsewhere that whoever fears God and does what is right is acceptable to Him, the meaning is not that a heathen, *as* a heathen, is capable of fearing God uprightly or doing genuine works of godliness. For "whatever does not proceed from faith is sin," Romans 14, the last verse. Rather, it is only meant to indicate that in the joyful times of the New Testament, the distinction between Jews and heathens has been entirely abolished, and that the latter, if they make use of the <term>means of salvation</term> <note>original: "Heyls-Mittel"; in Lutheran theology, these are the instruments through which God offers grace, specifically the Word of God and the Sacraments.</note>, have no less right to the grace of **GOD** and eternal life than the former.

What, then, do people commonly cite to justify this prejudice? Especially this: that over the passing of many years, hardly anyone from other religions turns to the Lutheran faith. They argue that this would not happen if its truth were so clear and distinct. I must confess that, alas! certainly more people leave the God-pleasing Lutheran faith than those of other religious backgrounds embrace it. But how can one use this unfortunate trend to belittle the true religion? It has always been the fashion of the world that frivolous people love lies and darkness more than truth and light. 

One can prove this irrefutably from all of history. Furthermore, there is no doubt that many adhere outwardly to other religions but reject and condemn in their hearts what they profess for appearance's sake. These people would have no hesitation in crossing over from lies to the truth, if not for the base love of the world and the fear of expected physical misery placing a heavy obstacle in their way.

### One should not make so much difficulty in reaching a religious union with the Reformed.

# ...with the Reformed, a Religion &c.

departed from Luther's party, being called both Zwinglians and Calvinists. And such names are certainly applied to them with justice, as they do not hesitate to agree with and accept their teachings. Furthermore, one can well grant them the eagerly sought name of the **Reformed**, if by that one understands such people who have torn themselves away from the unbearable yoke of the **Papacy** <note>the Roman Catholic Church system</note> and have to some extent purified the doctrines of faith. At this point, the question remains whether the Lutherans should not unite with them again and enter into a fellowship? **Philipp** <note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560), Luther’s closest collaborator, known for his more conciliatory stance toward the Reformed</note> wished for it so longingly that he often wrote to good friends: If he were to shed as many hot tears as there is water to be found in the **Elbe** <note>a major river in Germany flowing through Wittenberg</note>, he would still not be able to express the most sensitive pain that has grown in his soul over these disputes. *e)* Other upright men of the orthodox church have also hitherto voiced similar complaints and heartily wished for a blessed union of both parties, but out of love for the truth have also always unashamedly confessed that such a thing—as long as the Reformed do not abandon their current doctrines—is utterly impossible and not to be hoped for. Yet many, especially among **statesmen** and **scholars**, hold quite a different opinion and have allowed themselves to be taken in by the dangerous prejudice that the Lutherans should rightly give in to the Reformed and [regard] them as fellow believers...

->§. 2.<-

Every person can easily judge for themselves where this prejudice originates. On the one hand, opportunity is given by the frequent requests in which the Reformed themselves have sought union with the Lutherans. **Zwingli** <note>Huldrych Zwingli (1484–1531), the leader of the Reformation in Switzerland</note> made it a great priority at the **Colloquy of Marburg** <note>a famous 1529 meeting intended to unite the two Protestant factions; it failed over a disagreement regarding the nature of the Lord's Supper</note> to persuade **Luther** to recognize him as a brother in faith. Luther himself writes of this: Zwingli said publicly in the presence of the **Landgrave** <note>Philip I of Hesse, who hosted the Marburg meeting</note> while shedding the bitterest tears: **"There are no people on earth with whom I would rather be at one than with those of Wittenberg."** <note>original: "Wittenbergern"</note> *f)* **Beza** <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a French Protestant theologian and successor to John Calvin</note> sought the same with earnest entreaty during the meeting arranged in 1586 at **Montbéliard** <note>original: "Mümpelgard"</note> between him and **Dr. Jakob Andreae** <note>a primary author of the Lutheran Formula of Concord</note>; and when the latter had deep hesitations about extending the right hand of brotherhood to him, Beza then also rejected the offered right hand of friendship. *g)* The well-known **Dr. Johannes Crocius** <note>a prominent 17th-century Reformed theologian</note> uses quite moving words on this subject: "Peace be with you," he says, "dear brothers in Christ, otherwise called Lutherans—all you who call upon the name of the LORD JESUS with us, and who desire to be saved through His death and bloodshed just as we do! Whether you wish it or not, you are our brothers—though long-contending and divided, yet truly and by right."

So hateful to the troublesome Satan is the purity of the Evangelical doctrine <note>In this 18th-century context, "Evangelical" refers specifically to the Lutheran Church.</note> that he strives for nothing more than to hinder its emergence. They deceive themselves like ignorant children, who think the sun is a very small light compared to the moon, when in fact the moon has no light of its own, except insofar as it is shared with it by the sun. Since the **Socinians** <term>Socinians: followers of a movement founded by Laelius and Faustus Socinus which denied the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ, emphasizing rationalism</term> do not consider themselves bound to believe anything except what their natural understanding dictates to them—and moreover, only agree with divine **Revelation** insofar as it aligns with that understanding—it is no wonder that they attempt to excuse this religion and exalt it with their foolish praises. *Like rejoices in like* <note>original Latin: "Par pari gaudet"</note>; birds of a feather flock together. 

However, if the simple and unlearned are burdened with this preconceived opinion, they allow themselves to be led astray by the mere appearance of **Godliness**. Indeed, one must grant the Socinians this fame—if it can indeed be called fame—that they carry themselves as quite godly and virtuous in their outward appearance. And they do this all the more because they believe that by doing so, they make themselves worthy of the grace of GOD and divine rewards. Therefore, they commonly present themselves as "precious temples" constructed and assembled from nothing but holiness and virtue.

so delicate that it refuses to consider any single religion as correct and consistent with the truth in every single point. Therefore, according to their declaration, one should find something good in every religion, though more in some than in others. And many count the so-called Arminian religion among this latter kind, which received its name from Jacobus Arminius. In his youth, he was a very poor and lowly person, but possessed a quite exceptional spirit and intellectual gifts. Hence, while staying at a public inn in his hometown of Oudewater <note>A city in the Utrecht province of the Netherlands</note> and serving those who visited there, he showed many signs of his capable mind and clever intellect, whereby some compassionate hearts were moved to gift this poor man generously, thus freeing him from the tedious service of the inn. Following this, he dedicated himself entirely to his studies and successfully continued them, especially since the Council of Amsterdam supported him with scholarships. *a)* He achieved such a fine understanding of both divine and worldly matters that, after he had gathered the treasures of exceptional scholarship in Leiden, Marburg, Geneva, Basel, Padua, and other places, he was appointed to a preaching position by the Council of Amsterdam in the year 1582. *b)* His particular merits were such that, when the Academy of Leiden suffered a significant <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "Scha-" suggests the next word is "Schaden," meaning "loss" or "damage."</note>

In the meantime, as his followers were increasingly persecuted by the heated **Gomarists** <gloss>the strict Calvinist followers of Franciscus Gomarus</gloss>, they submitted a humble petition in the year 1610, titled the **Remonstrance** <note>original: "Remonstrantiam"</note>, to the **States of Holland**. In response, the zealous Calvinists did not rest, but drafted another document which they called the **Counter-Remonstrance** <note>original: "Contra-Remonstrantiam"</note>. From that time on, the followers of Arminius were called **Remonstrants**, while the other Reformed members who sided with Gomarus were called **Counter-Remonstrants**. These hated names caused a violent disruption and bitterness of spirit, so much so that even the great **King of Britain** <note>King James I (r. 1603–1625), who was deeply interested in the theological stability of the Protestant world</note> could easily foresee the troubling consequences <note>original: "Sviten," from the French "suites," meaning results or developments</note> to be feared. [...is most con]venient. <note>The text begins by completing the word "convenientissimus" from the previous page's catchword.</note> We call the genuine and literal sense not so much that which the actual words indicate (as often happens), but rather that which—even if the exact words do not explicitly carry it—nevertheless most closely agrees with sound reason and the mind and purpose of the writer or speaker. *gg)* <term>Curcelläus <note>Étienne de Courcelles (1586–1659), a prominent Remonstrant theologian and scholar who succeeded Simon Episcopius at the Amsterdam seminary.</note></term> holds the same doctrine, for he says: <note>original Latin: "Rationis est expendere, quis genuinus loci alicujus controversi sensus sit, aut quæ mens Dei nos in Scriptura alloquentis. Quod adeo necessarium est, ut nullam ex sacræ Scripturæ lectione utilitatem percipere possimus, nisi ad illius intelligentiam rationem in consilium adhibeamus."</note> It belongs to reason to weigh what the genuine sense of any controversial passage may be, or what is the mind of God addressing us in Scripture. This is so necessary that we can perceive no benefit from reading Holy Scripture unless we call reason into council for its understanding. It is the role of sound reason to consider what the true understanding of a disputed passage of Scripture might be, or what the meaning is of God speaking to us in the Scripture. ### [On Imputation and Righteousness]

<meta>catchword: they</meta>

Here they contend <note>original Latin: *hic digladiantur*—literally "to fence with swords," implying a fierce scholarly debate.</note> whether only Christ's **passive righteousness** <term>Passive righteousness: The merit Christ earned through his suffering and death.</term>, or indeed also his **active righteousness** <term>Active righteousness: The merit Christ earned by perfectly obeying God's Law throughout his life.</term> is imputed <note>original: *imputetur*; legally credited to a person's account.</note> to us, although Scripture does not utter a single word about it. The righteousness that is imputed to us is not the righteousness of Christ: for the Scripture teaches nowhere that the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us; but only that faith is imputed to us for righteousness, and indeed for Christ’s sake. Therefore, those are foolish people who fight vehemently over whether it is solely the righteousness of Christ that is imputed to us—which he earned through his actions or his suffering—when Scripture does not mention either with a single word. Rather, it is much more a gracious esteeming and acceptance of our own imperfect righteousness (which, if God wished to proceed strictly against us, could not stand before the court) as a perfect righteousness, for the sake of Jesus Christ.

# The Arminian Religion Seems
<meta>catchword: ver-</meta>

...touched upon <note>original: *rühret*; the text begins mid-sentence, concluding a point from the previous page.</note>. But I do not doubt that every impartial mind will be able to sufficiently conclude from the facts cited that it is so far from the truth that the Arminian religion <term>Arminianism: A theological movement that arose in the early 17th century, emphasizing human free will and questioning strict predestination.</term> can be held as one of the best; rather, it must rightly be numbered among the very worst. What is more irresponsible than to extend freedom of faith so far that everyone should be permitted to believe and teach whatever he wants? Truly, if a gardener were so careless and allowed all the emerging weeds in his garden to take root, it would be feared that these would finally ruin all the good trees and fruits. 

Granted also that the Arminian religion greatly flatters human reason <note>original: *Vernunfft*</note>; should it therefore be considered particularly good? Upright Christians always cherish the greatest reverence for those doctrines of faith which appear most difficult and incomprehensible to reason. # ...to be one of the very best.

...capable of making a bad religion good: since the soul of true religion consists alone in an unadulterated and correct faith. <header>Quietism is by no means as evil,</header>

## XII. Prejudice.

### Quietism is by no means as evil as it is denounced, but rather worthy of praise and acceptance.

->§. 1.<-

Church history proves sufficiently that the name of the "Quietists" was already known and common in ancient times; specifically, those were labeled with it who, out of a particular love for tranquility and a holy life, withdrew into solitude. There, they turned their minds away from all earthly things and sought to enjoy a perfect foretaste of blessed eternity while still in this world. *a)* <note>The author likely refers to early Christian desert monastics or anchorites.</note> After that time, in the 14th century, a certain type of holy person arose in Macedonia who made much of nothing but a noble soul-rest <term>soul-rest: or "Seelen-Ruhe," a state of inner stillness and peace</term>. They furthermore boasted that once they had entirely withdrawn their thoughts from the earthly, they were capable of peering closely into the greatest mysteries of the Godhead. They claimed their understanding would be filled with a special light—which they were accustomed to call the "Taboritic" light <note>original: "Taboritische"; referring to the Light of Mount Tabor, a concept in Hesychasm (Eastern Orthodox mysticism) regarding the light seen by the Apostles at the Transfiguration of Jesus</note>—and their soul would taste an incomprehensible enjoyment of divine sweetness. *b)* Finally, this name has come into fashion again recently, since the famous Molinos <note>Miguel de Molinos (1628–1696), a Spanish priest whose mystical teachings emphasizing inner passivity were later condemned by the Catholic Church</note> in Italy spread similar teachings, which solely—

aimed solely at inner peace of soul and complete <term>serenity: or "Gelassenheit," a state of detachment and surrender to God's will</term> in all circumstances. This Michael de Molinos, a Spaniard by birth, hailing from the Kingdom of Aragon, where he was born on December 21, 1640, in Patacina, had—despite his distinguished family—dedicated himself to the priesthood and was ordained as a secular priest <note>A "secular priest" lives in the world among the people, rather than within a monastic order.</note> in Pamplona. However, he conducted himself in this office in such a way that he neither accepted any income nor sought to draw people to himself as others of his order were accustomed to do. Nevertheless, he gained a quite remarkable following, especially in Italy, where he traveled in the year 1670 after having previously been promoted to Doctor at Coimbra. In Spain, he had studied <term>mystical theology</term> <note>original: "Theologiam mysticam"; a branch of theology focused on the soul's direct, subjective union with the Divine</note>, which was held in great esteem there because of Saint <term>Teresa</term> <note>original: "Teresiæ"; referring to Teresa of Ávila (1515–1582), the Spanish mystic and reformer</note>; and in Italy <note>original: "Welschland"; a historical German term for Latin or Romance-speaking lands, specifically Italy in this context</note> he now allowed the fruits of this to be seen through a serene, quiet, and virtuous way of life. This drew an incredible multitude of people, from both high and low stations, to him. The great Cardinals Casanate, Azzolino, Carpegna, Colloredo, Ciceri, Petruzzi, d'Estrées, and others held this supposedly godly man in high and worthy regard. People maintained an industrious correspondence with him from all sorts of cities and countries, so much so that on the very day he was taken into custody, twenty <term>Reichsthaler</term> <note>A large silver coin used throughout the Holy Roman Empire; twenty would be a significant sum for daily postage.</note> in postage fees had to be paid to the postmaster; and among his effects, more than 20,000 letters addressed to him were found,

received such approval that hardly six years had passed when it was printed more than twenty times in various languages. But because the interests of the <term>clergy</term> <note>The formal leadership and ordained ministers of the Church.</note> were noticeably weakened by this—since the people who were won over by Molinos’s principles insisted only on internal worship and made little account of the Mass and other Popish matters—it happened that the <term>Jesuits</term> <note>A religious order known for its political influence and role in the Counter-Reformation.</note> and <term>Dominicans</term> <note>A religious order often associated with the office of the Inquisition.</note> in particular sought to lay snares for Molinos. They slandered him at the Papal court in the worst possible way; although entirely in vain and fruitlessly. Indeed, Pope Innocent XI held him in such high regard that he granted him his own apartment in his palace.

Given this state of affairs, his enemies thought it advisable to take another path; they sought the support of the King of France’s confessor, <term>Father de la Chaise</term> <note>François de la Chaise (1624–1709), the influential Jesuit confessor to King Louis XIV.</note>, and brought it so far that the said King had serious representations made to the Pope to abolish and suppress this <term>heresy</term> <note>A belief or doctrine that deviates from established Church dogma.</note>. The Pope, though reluctantly, had to allow the Court of the <term>Inquisition</term> <note>The ecclesiastical tribunal responsible for the discovery and punishment of heresy.</note> to take over the investigation of this matter. Molinos was taken prisoner along with his followers; even Innocent XI himself had to give an account of his faith to a deputation sent by the Inquisition. And after the other prisoners had been released, the judgment was passed on Molinos that he should be condemned to perpetual imprisonment, in which he lived for 9 years, and finally in the year 1696.

<page-num>290</page-num>
### Quietism is by no means so evil, ###

He died on the 28th of December, 1696: whereupon this epitaph was prepared for him: ->"Here lies the body of **Dr. Molinos**, the great heretic!"<- <note>original: "Quie il Corpo del D. Molinos gran Hæret. Hie ist der Leib des D. Molinos des grossen Ketzers!"</note> From this man, today’s **Quietism** <note>A movement emphasizing internal stillness and a passive state of the soul to achieve union with God.</note> received its origin and name; because its primary doctrine consisted in this: that a person must strive solely and exclusively for the inner peace of the soul. Although things went quite harshly for him and his followers, there was never a lack of those who warmed up his principles once again. In particular, the excellent Archbishop of Cambray, **Francis de Salignac Fénelon**, who passed away only last year <note>Fénelon died in 1715, suggesting this text was written around 1716.</note>, became very well known through this. In the year 1698, he published his book, which he titled **Explanation of the Maxims of the Saints on the Interior Life** <note>original French: "Explication des Maximes des Saints sur la Vie interieure"</note>; and this caused no small stir among his fellow believers. ### §. 5.

Furthermore, one finds a great multitude of dangerous errors within Quietistic <term>Quietism: a 17th-century mystical movement that taught that perfection is found in the complete passivity of the soul</term> theology. According to their opinion, the whole of theology should be contemplative and consist purely of meditation; even though Scripture demands that everything in theology must aim toward practice <term>praxis: the practical application of faith through deeds and moral living</term>. The Savior does not praise those who hear His teachings, but those who also act upon them, John 13:17. And the ancient teacher Justin <note>Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD), an early Christian apologist.</note> writes: *The matters of our religion consist not in words, but in deeds* <note>original Latin: "Res Religionis nostræ non in verbis, sed in factis consistunt"</note>. They claim that mystical theology should be entirely preferred over common theology, as it supposedly contains the true and proper heavenly wisdom in its most perfect form; however, I shall shortly demonstrate that such a claim is false and groundless. Therefore, whoever was eager to attain the fame of a holiness pleasing to GOD sought to distinguish and signalize himself through Mystical writings.

# XIV. Prejudice.

Even in his own time, the blessed Luther was concerned that one day wretched Epicureanism <note>In this context, a disregard for divine law in favor of worldly pleasure or atheistic indifference.</note> and Enthusiasm <note>Commonly known in German as *Schwärmerei*; the belief that one receives direct, personal revelations from God that override or supplement the Bible.</note> would cause great harm to the Christian religion, and would so prevail that the world, instead of true holiness, would practice nothing but a wicked existence, and instead of the pure and clear Word of God, would put forward its own dreams. *a*) What this otherwise joyful hero of faith feared back then, we unfortunately seem to have lived to see. # The Doctrine of the Fanatics is Unobjectionable <note>The header "unverwerfflich" likely refers to how these doctrines appear to the uncritical eye or is part of a larger polemical argument. ...this method was primarily used by the Roman King Numa Pompilius <note>Numa Pompilius was the legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing many of the city's religious and political institutions.</note> and the world-renowned Muhammad as a political maneuver <term>Staats-Streich: a stroke of statecraft or political trick</term> to keep the people in blind obedience. # XV. Prejudice.
## The sect of the so-called Quakers is not as evil as they are accused of being.

-> §. I. <-

**A**lthough the Quakers certainly belong among the enthusiasts and <term>fanatics</term> <note>original German: "Schwärmer," a derogatory term used by established churches for radical reformers who "swarmed" like bees around new ideas.</note>, of whom I have already dealt elsewhere; I must nevertheless speak here specifically about them in a bit more detail, because I perceive that many are of the opinion that this is not such an evil, erroneous, and damnable sect as is commonly stated by our teachers. They derive their name from the English word "quake," which is said to mean to tremble and shake, and thus a "Quaker" in our dialect means as much as a "Trembler" or "Shaker." The origin of this name is said to come from this: when their founder George Fox was summoned before the court to give an account regarding the division he had stirred up and other improper dealings, he is said to have constantly cried out to the judges: **Tremble before the word of God!** His reckless followers did the same here and there. Indeed, they admit that the name fits them because of the quaking and trembling that occurs among many of them. For the learned men who have personally associated with these people testify unanimously that, both in public assemblies and in their private homes, they often suddenly begin to tremble violently while speaking and appear as if they were <term>entranced</term> <note>original German: "entzücket," referring to a state of religious ecstasy or trance.</note>, which is quite terrifying to behold. *c)* This, they say, stems from the light shining and flashing with full brilliance into their souls, which is impossible for them to endure; thus it causes an unusual trembling of the limbs, a heavy foaming of the lips, and an unruly posture of the body. *d)*

->§. 2.<-

Dear reader, where does this come from? It is easy to guess: the world is always eager for something new. New lies please it better than old truths. To the world, the latter seems like something common; the former, something extraordinary. Furthermore, the world is eager to possess the reputation of holiness. If as much zeal were applied to living virtuously and holily as is spent on *seeming* virtuous and holy, certainly piety would be so prevalent that one would find no reason to repeat the lament with David: **Help, Lord, for the godly are no more; the faithful have vanished from among the children of men, Psalm 12, verse 2.** Yet what is more repugnant to <term>flesh and blood</term> <note>A biblical idiom referring to human nature in its fallible, unregenerate state, often contrasted with spiritual discipline.</note> than being holy in actual deed? The world’s contempt and enmity, and the beloved Cross <note>The "Cross" represents the specific trials and social suffering a believer is expected to endure for their faith.</note> which follows the holy children of God at every step, tastes far too harsh and bitter. To constantly search the Divine Word and to obtain faith from it—for without faith, holiness is but a dream, and indeed even sin—and to learn the correct ways of God is a tedious task. The easier a thing is, the more it appeals to human laziness. The more prestige it grants before others, the more sinful pride seeks it. But what is easier than boasting of one’s own godliness? What charms...

<page-num>365</page-num>
<sig>S. 3.</sig>

...not as evil as they are accused of being.

What appeals to the ignorant more than the outward appearance of holiness? To see into the heart is a superhuman matter. He who can present himself as the most holy is commonly regarded as the holiest. This causes so many to chase after the appearance of a godly nature. And it is certainly a convenient means to reach one's goal with the unwary when one praises the Quakers and extols their teachings. For these people, in all their actions, strive for the appearance of perfection in sanctification. They even reject things as highly sinful which the Spirit of God Himself classifies as <term>indifferent matters</term> <note>original: "Mittel-Dinge." In theology, these are "adiaphora"—actions that are neither commanded nor forbidden by God, such as specific styles of dress or social customs.</note>. They disapprove not only of the abuse of oaths, dancing, compliments, and the pleasures of the body and mind, but also of their permissible use; in doing so, they <note>A German idiom: "schütten solchergestalt das Kind mit dem Bade aus."</note> throw the baby out with the bathwater. This draws people's eyes to them. This awakens wonder; this makes a special name for them. What wonder is it, then, that one is so easily misled into having high regard for the Quakers. To this are added other circumstances. People think: the Quakers endure the harshest persecutions with calm steadfastness; they have no self-interest in their teaching; their sect has spread in a truly miraculous way; kings and high-ranking people of the nation have been well-disposed toward them; surely, they cannot have such evil ways.

<summary>The author explains that the Quakers gain followers because their strict rejection of even harmless social customs creates a false impression of extreme holiness. He notes that their steadfastness under persecution and their rapid growth lead many to wrongly assume their doctrines are sound.</summary>

And certainly, if it depended on the judgment of our ill-behaved pseudo-Lutherans <note>original: "After-Lutheraner"—the prefix "after" was used pejoratively in this period to denote something sham, false, or degenerate.</note>, there would be no better cause than that of the Quakers. For they praise their writings as pure essence and power <note>original: "Safft und Krafft"—literally "juice and strength," a common idiom for something full of vitality and meaning.</note>: their doctrine as pure heavenly wisdom: their life as a noble pattern of piety. If their transgressions and fanaticisms <note>original: "Schwärmereyen"—a highly charged term used by mainstream reformers to describe those who claimed direct, emotional, or mystical inspiration from the Holy Spirit outside of scripture.</note> are too great, it is said: Zeal for the Lord caused them to stumble a little: an unthinking word often escapes a child zealous for his father’s honor: the great amount of good found in them more than covers the small spots of their failings. They recommend Barclay’s *Theses* and *Apology* <note>referring to Robert Barclay (1648–1690) and his work *An Apology for the True Christian Divinity* (1678), the primary systematic defense of Quaker theology.</note> as a model according to which theology should be structured and presented: in them, one would not find so many useless scholastic whims; instead, everything is presented clearly according to the Bible: why, then, does the same not happen among us?

...ritual body, and must be understood as a spiritual body, but not as that body or temple of Christ which was born of the Virgin Mary, and in which he walked, lived, and suffered in the land of Judea. *ppp)* All of this, however, falls completely away when one considers that nowhere in Scripture is a spiritual body attributed to Christ, but only a fleshly and human one. Because he was God alone before this body was assigned to him, and since God is a spirit, one cannot assign a spiritual body to him. Not to mention that a "spiritual body" is such a figure of speech that, by its own addition, completely cancels the subject out (it is, namely, a contradiction in terms <note>original: "est scilicet Contradictio in adjecto" — a logic term for when an adjective contradicts the noun it describes, like "square circle."</note>).

However, anyone would be greatly deceived if they imagined that these were all the errors of the **Quaker sect**. For I have, so to speak, only recounted their most common principles, from each of which—as if from a poisonous spring—many other specific errors flow. Nevertheless, it would require too much space if I wanted to add even brief remarks to each of the points mentioned above. Meanwhile, because many people praise the Quakers primarily for the fact that they so carefully avoid and disapprove of all outward pomp, all pleasures, titles of honor, and the like—and perhaps even develop a high regard for them based on this disdain—I cannot help but share my modest thoughts on the matter.

It must indeed be considered sinful and displeasing to the Most High. But should this abominable abuse mean that one is not permitted to call a king **Your Majesty**, a prince **Your Serene Highness**, and so forth? No, the Scripture in no way disapproves of it; rather, it commands it in the Fourth Commandment. For the wise **Sirach** <note>Also known as Ecclesiasticus, a book of the Apocrypha highly regarded in the Lutheran tradition</note> explains this commandment very well: that one should honor parents—that is, all superiors and those in authority—"in deed and in word" <note>original: "ἔργῳ καὶ λόγῳ"</note>, **Sirach 3:9.** **Peter** says: **Honor the King, 1 Pet. 2:17.** **Paul** gives the exhortation to give honor to whom honor is due, **Rom. 13:7.** In all these passages, one finds no specific formulas prescribed for use; but by this very fact, the Spirit of God intended to teach us that we should respect custom and use such titles as are common in a commonwealth <note>original: "Republic," referring here to the organized state or community</note>, provided they do not detract from the honor of God. Indeed, what is more? One even finds important titles in the Scripture itself that are given to the authorities and even to private individuals. God Himself calls kings and princes "gods" and "children of the Most High," because they represent God’s place as ambassadors and uphold God’s judgment, **Ps. 92:6.** <note>The author likely refers to Psalm 82:6, where rulers are called "gods" (*elohim*); biblical numbering often varied in early modern texts</note> Who would deny that this says just as much, indeed even more, than **Your Majesty** or **Your Serenity**? And why should one begrudge them this title, since God speaks of them: **You, Nebuchadnezzar, are a king...**

->§. 9.<-

From this you can now see the true nature of the Quakers. Therefore, do not let it lead you astray when they seem to disguise themselves as nothing but angels of light in their manner of living; it is enough that their teaching originates from the father of lies <note>A biblical reference to the Devil, based on John 8:44</note>. If you will consider this fairly, and additionally consult the writings published against this sect, such as:

1) The *Quaker Abominations* <note>original German: "Quäcker-Greuel"</note> by the Right Reverend Ministry of Hamburg.
2) Dr. Zentgravius’s *The Quaker Sink* <note>original Latin: "Colluviem Quackerorum"; referring to a collection of filth or a moral drain</note>.
3) Dr. Schelwigius’s *Quakerism Refuted* <note>original Latin: "Qvakerismum confutatum"</note>.
4) *Against Barclay* <note>original Latin: "Anti-Barclajum"; a response to Robert Barclay, the primary theologian of the early Quaker movement</note> by Misters Anton Reiser and Holzhausen.
5) Dr. Neumann’s *Synopsis of the Errors of Fanatics or Tremblers* <note>original Latin: "Synopsin Errorum Fanaticorum s. Tremulorum"; "Tremblers" was a literal translation and often a mocking term for Quakers</note>.
6) Mr. Figken’s *History of the Fanatics* <note>original Latin: "Historiam Fanaticorum"</note>.
7) Mr. Richard Baxter’s *Quaker Catechism*.
8) Mr. Lassenius and others on the *Brood of New Swarmers* <note>"Swarmers" (German: Schwarm-Geister) was a derogatory term used by Lutherans since the time of Luther to describe those they believed followed their own "spirit" rather than Scripture</note>.

# XVI. Prejudice.
## Cartesian Theology seems to be the very safest.

->§. 1.<-

Among the learned, one will not easily find anyone to whom the great philosopher René Descartes <note>original Latin: *Renatus Cartesius*</note> is not known. Indeed, his knowledge in worldly matters was so exceptional, and his diligence which he applied to the investigation of truth so remarkable, that one would commit the highest injustice if one did not hold proper respect for this excellent man. *a) It would have been shameful for France to lack esteem for a man who brought her so much honor, and whose name is held in such high regard among foreigners.* <note>original French: "Il auroit ete honteux pour la France de manquer d'estime pour un homme, qui luy a fait tant d'honeur, & dont le nom est en si grande consideration chez les étrangers."</note> Such was the judgment passed on him in his time by the well-read Mr. Louis Moréri <note>Louis Moréri (1643–1680) was a French priest and encyclopedist famous for his historical dictionary</note>: It would be a great disgrace to France if it did not wish to highly value such a man, who brought it such great honor, and whose name is held in high regard even among foreigners. *b)* And I may well say, it would be detrimental to all lovers of truth if they did not hold in due honor a man who discovered so many truths, or at least paved the way to successfully finding many more. This world-famous philosopher was a Frenchman by birth, born in La Haye in the <term>Touraine</term> <note>A traditional province of France; Descartes' birthplace is now renamed "Descartes" in his honor</note>, where in the year 1596, the

<summary>This page introduces a critique of Cartesianism by first acknowledging the immense intellectual reputation of René Descartes and the respect he commanded across Europe. The author cites Louis Moréri to emphasize that Descartes was a source of national pride for France and a pivotal figure in the search for truth.</summary>

<page-num>402</page-num>
<header>Cartesian Theology</header>

...born on March 31st to distinguished noble parents. *c)* Even in his tender youth, he already displayed such a strong love for the knowledge of truth and such a diligent investigation into the causes of natural things that his father, Joachim Descartes, was accustomed to jokingly calling him "his philosopher" <note>original Latin: *Philosophum*</note>. *d)* To nurture this desire and to make such a sharp-witted son a useful instrument for the state <note>original: *Republique*</note>, he was placed in the college <note>original: *Versammlung*, referring to the Jesuit College of La Flèche</note> of the Jesuits. In learning the studies common there, he gave his teachers complete satisfaction; his mind, however, was very poorly satisfied with them all. In most of the subjects that were usually presented, he could find hardly a slight probability, much less a clear truth.

To that end, he resolved to abandon all previously accepted principles and to research the truth of every matter through his own reflection. In this endeavor, he seemed to be somewhat hindered, both by the dissolute company into which he fell and by the military life <note>original: *Kriegs-Wesen*</note> he entered. Yet, when these two obstacles were successfully cleared away, he retired into quiet solitude to pursue his contemplations more undisturbed. He spent twenty-five years in such a life near Egmond in Holland, until Queen Christina finally had him come to her in Sweden, where...

He stood in such high favor with the Queen that he remained at her bedside for many nights, having the honor of entertaining her with his discourses, until he finally concluded his life in the year 1650. *e)* Although his life thus lasted no more than 54 years, he nevertheless discovered so much of merit in that short time, or retrieved and explained it from the ancient philosophers <note>original German: *Welt-Weisen*</note>, *f)* that even his own enemies cannot help but accord him great fame. ## Cartesian Theology

...[sharp-witted]ness and clarity of speech, and he dispelled in many places the darkness that ignorance and barbarism had brought into natural science. <note>Original Latin: *tia, ac perspicuitate dictionis, & dispulerit in nonnullis tenebras, quas in scientiam naturalem inscities & Barbaries induxerati*</note> May the name of Descartes <note>referred to here by his Latinized name, Cartesius</note> remain in high esteem for more than a century; may he be held among the most eminent in <term>Geometry</term> and <term>Dioptrics</term> <note>the study of how light refracts through lenses</note>; may his writings be diligently read throughout the whole world; let him be praised for his sharp-wittedness, successful inventions, tireless investigation, and clarity in speech and writing, and for having dispelled the darkness that had penetrated natural philosophy through ignorance and barbarism. *i)* Indeed, although some insolent slanderers have mockingly called this great man a "philosopher of card" <note>original French: *par raillerie Philosophe de Carte*, a pun on his name implying he was a "paper" or "flimsy" philosopher</note> or a paper-philosopher; *k)* sensible people will nonetheless not be moved by this to pass any judgment on him other than what he deserves. 

Just as experience frequently confirms that the most sharp-witted and capable minds most easily offend against holy theology—especially when they trust themselves to grasp and understand everything through their own diligence, without the assistance and contribution of others—so too is this evident from the example of Descartes. Inasmuch as it cannot be denied that he certainly mixed many dangerous propositions, intolerable to pure theology <note>original German: *Gottes-Gelehrheit*</note>, into his writings, even though he frequently declared that he did not wish to involve himself in theological disputes at all, much less to subject them to the scrutiny of reason—

*l)* Meanwhile, I must also say this: Descartes himself did not make matters nearly as tangled or chaotic as his successors did. *m)* These followers consistently adapted the philosophical propositions of their teacher to theology; they wished to test and measure everything by the **Scales of Reason**, rather than the **Scales of the Sanctuary** <note>A metaphor for the Bible or divine authority as the ultimate standard of truth</note>. It is therefore no wonder that the author of the *Paradoxical Exercises on Philosophy as the Interpreter of Scripture* <note>Original Latin: *Exercitationis paradoxæ de Philosophia Scripturæ interprete*; a controversial work arguing that philosophy should be the primary tool for biblical interpretation</note> (who is said to be Lodewijk Meyer in Amsterdam), along with Christophorus Wittichius, Abraham Heidanus, Frans Burman, Petrus Allinga, Lodewijk Wolzogen, Jo. de Raye, Alhardus de Raadt, Adrianus Heereboord, Jacobus Golius, and many others *n)* have brought forth entirely absurd opinions that defile the purity of doctrine. 

Just as no food can be so spoiled that some gluttonous stomach would not feel a great appetite for it, so too there is no lack of people who find this corrupt **Cartesian theology** highly agreeable. This is despite the fact that such theology is clearly inconsistent with the guideline of God's Word. For this reason, even during Descartes’ lifetime, the Curators of **Leiden University** <note>The prestigious Dutch university where Cartesianism first caused major academic and religious friction</note> issued a reminder to him to refrain from theological disputes from then on. *o)* Furthermore, the States of Holland, as well as the **Synod** <note>A formal council of church leaders</note> held in Delft in the year 1657, later placed a forceful restraint on these Cartesian theologians. *p)* Nevertheless, curious minds in great numbers still strive...

<header>Cartesian Theology</header>

[num]ber who speak in its favor and praise it as the most certain doctrine of all.

->§. 2.<-

Without doubt, they are prompted to do this partly because it is meant to be something new, and partly because it opens the boundaries of **Reason** <note>German: *Vernunfft*</note> quite wide and permits more freedom than is proper. Generally, the newer a thing is, the more **approval** <note>Original: *Approbation*</note> it tends to find. If a new fashion in clothing arises, no one wants to be satisfied with the old anymore. What seemed lovely and beautiful to everyone a hundred years ago now appears quite simple and contemptible to the world. We see this in the **people of Israel**: even they finally grew weary of the eternal and infinite God, and therefore demanded of **Aaron** that he should make them new gods—whom they then worshipped with greater displays of joy than they had ever shown toward the true God. Since **Cartesian theology** now flatters these inconstant minds with the appearance of **novelty**, they allow themselves to be thoughtlessly seduced into listening to it. They lavishly bestow upon it that high esteem which actually belongs to the pure doctrine drawn from the clear **fountain of Israel** <note>A metaphor for the Bible and the original, untainted teachings of the faith</note>. It is a testimony that no "giddy spirit" <note>original German: "Schwindel-Geist" — referring to someone whose mind is spinning with confused or erratic ideas.</note> is capable of overturning. # Cartesian Theology

Reason indeed teaches that the more fluid and flowing a **body** <note>original: "Corpus"</note> is, the more mobile it is; conversely, the thicker and harder it is, the less it is inclined toward motion. Now, if a sensible **mathematician** <note>original: "Mathematicus"</note> were to make a comparison between the fact that the Earth is much smaller than the Sun, and the Sun’s fluid—and consequently most suitable for motion—nature, he would perhaps see that one has no cause to cry out against the motion of the Earth as an incomprehensible thing. Yet the senses themselves seem to quite strongly refute the assertions of the **Cartesians** <term>Cartesians: Followers of René Descartes who supported the heliocentric (sun-centered) model</term> and **Copernicans**. If someone, for example, traveled from **East to West** <note>literally: "from morning toward evening"</note>, he would have to be knocked over every time he tried to set down a foot; for according to the calculations of the **astronomers**, the Earth must move several hundred miles in a single minute. 

But to tell the truth, this is what convinces me most of all of the falsehood of the Cartesian hypothesis: A **gunner** <note>original: "Canonierer"</note> aims his **mortar** <note>original: "Mortier"</note> at a certain target and throws the bomb to the place where he actually aimed. Now, it happens that he successfully reaches his goal, provided he is well-versed in his art. I ask: how could this be possible if the Earth were moved? The bomb will remain in the air for at least a minute; consequently, it would have to fall 300 miles away from the set target, because the Earth moves that much and even more in one minute. If one were to say: The **atmosphere** <note>original: "Atmosphæra"</note> would move at the same time as the Earth

# XVII. Prejudice.
## One must certainly grant the Cocceians the fame of being truly good theologians.

-> §. I. <-

That one holds the merits of learned people in due high esteem is required by the gratitude owed to them, and certainly deserves to be praised; but that one often oversteps the boundaries, and also elevates too highly and loves beyond measure that in which great people have erred significantly, is evident from the example of both the Cartesians and the Cocceians <note>The Cocceians were followers of Johannes Cocceius, who emphasized a "federal" or covenantal interpretation of the Bible, often aligning with Cartesian rationalism in the 17th century.</note>. # XVIII. Prejudice.
## Spinoza's doctrine is by no means as godless and evil as people claim.

->§. I.<-

Among those spirits who, driven by an excessive ambition, have sought to immortalize their names—and indeed established a lasting monument of their godlessness for posterity through their wicked conduct, though by no means achieving true glory—I may well count Benedict Spinoza <note>The original text uses the variation "Benedictum Spinolam."</note> first and foremost. Ambition led him so far astray that he sought to become immortal by discarding a doctrine believed for thousands of years, overturning all theology, and—as a famous teacher puts it—turning prophecy into the mere imagination of sick people, miracles into natural effects, sacred history into fictional tales, divine laws into the simple impulses of a necessarily acting Nature, and holiness into nothing but the deceptive dreams of men. <margin>a)</margin> He has also reached the point where, although all sensible and God-loving souls feel a loathing for his memory, his name nonetheless flourishes in the greatest veneration among those of his own kind. This freak of nature <note>original: "Abendtheuer der Natur." While "Abendtheuer" usually means "adventure," in this context it refers to a "monstrosity" or a "strange phenomenon" that deviates from the natural order.</note> was born in 1634 to Jewish parents who were engaged in trade in Amsterdam; and because he, in his youth... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "gend," likely part of a word like "genügsam" (sufficiently) or "gestanden" (stood) to be continued on the next page.</note>

He despised all wealth, and although significant presents were often offered to him, he refused to accept them every time, preferring to earn his living by grinding lenses <term>Glasschleiffen: the craft of grinding and polishing optical glass for spectacles and telescopes, which provided Spinoza a meager but independent income</term> with his own hand rather than live off the gifts of others. He was moderate in anger, composed in adversities, and affable toward everyone. He was an utter enemy to ostentatious clothing, claiming: a fine suit of clothes does not make a better man. He also thought nothing of banquets and debauchery, and while he could have enjoyed delicious food at the homes of others, he preferred to settle for the simplest fare at home in his cherished solitude. His discourses always seemed to aim at virtue and respectability, so much so that he several times encouraged the family of his landlord toward godliness, recommending that they listen to good preachers, and even frequently attended the sermons of Christian teachers himself, especially those of Dr. Cordes <note>original: "D. # XIX. Prejudice.
## The hoped-for thousand-year kingdom is a well-founded doctrine.

->§. 1.<-

I am by no means speaking here of the sweet dreams that the Jews envision regarding the still falsely expected arrival of the Messiah, in which they promise themselves a thousand types of delight and earthly pleasure in this world. For they claim that once the Messiah has gathered all the Jews together from all parts of the world, he will, as their King, treat them most magnificently and refresh them with the best animals and the noblest wine. Among other things, he will serve them the slaughtered <term>Shor Ha-bor</term> <note>original Hebrew: שור הבר; a mythical wild ox or Behemoth intended for a banquet at the end of time</note> or Behemoth, the terrifying whale <term>Leviathan</term>, along with his mate, and the great bird <term>Bar Juchne</term> <note>original Hebrew: בר יוכנה; a legendary giant bird in Talmudic folklore</note>. Along with this, there will be no lack of lovely games and other amusements, and more of such earthly things. **a)** Rather, I am speaking of such a thousand-year kingdom as so-called Christians claim and hope for.

hope, that the Savior who ascended into heaven shall visibly appear again on earth a thousand years before the general Final Judgment, overthrow all his enemies, gather the faithful to himself, and rule with them in full delight. When one collects all the <term>Chiliastic</term> <note>From the Greek 'chilias' meaning a thousand; the belief in a literal thousand-year reign of Christ on earth</note> writings, one must confess that it remains very difficult to draw from them a clear description or an exact sketch of this thousand-year kingdom. On the one hand, these writings are composed with such obscure words that one can easily see that the authors themselves must not have known what they wanted to write or say. Indeed, this is confirmed by manifold experience: most erroneous doctrines are usually clothed and hidden by their patrons in nothing but indistinct modes of speech and unintelligible flowery language <note>original: "Wort-Blumen"</note>, which admittedly sound pleasant at first to those with greedy and itching ears. However, if one considers the matter itself attentively and reflects on the words a bit more maturely, it is impossible to form a distinct and evident idea or concept of it. So it goes with most descriptions of the "newcomers" <note>likely referring to contemporary Pietists or radical reformers of the author's time</note> regarding the thousand-year kingdom. 

Dear reader! What is it actually supposed to mean when they call it the golden "Lily and Rose time," the "golden <term>Seculum</term>" <note>original Latin: 'seculum'; meaning an age, era, or century</note> <term>etc.</term>? One sees quite easily that this verbal artifice <note>original: "Wort-Drechslerey," literally 'word-turning,' implying something over-crafted and hollow like lathed wood</note> does not stem from the school of the Holy Spirit, but rather from a brain entirely devastated by vain dreams.

# The hoped-for thousand-year kingdom

On the other hand, it is also for this reason: because the originators and defenders of this kingdom are not in agreement among themselves as to what it should actually consist of. One concept of it was held by the notorious <term>sect-leader</term> <note>original: "Rotten-Meister," a derogatory term for a leader of a faction or heretical group</note> Cerinthus; another by the unreflective Papias and his followers; yet another is fashioned by the modern admirers of this presumed kingdom; and those who disclose their thoughts under the hope of "better times" present it in yet another portrait. How could it be otherwise? When one chooses to form all sorts of thoughts about spiritual things outside of and against the Holy Scripture, these thoughts must necessarily turn out to be unequal, contradictory, and adventurous. Whatever is measured by a standard unit <note>original: "nach einer Elle," referring to an ell, a historical unit of length</note> will be equal and similar to one another. But since every <term>Chiliast</term> <note>From the Greek 'chilias' (thousand); a believer in a literal 1,000-year earthly reign of Christ</note> measures the hoped-for earthly kingdom of Christ according to the scale of his own untamed imagination—and this cannot possibly be the same for each and every person—then the assertions of one must certainly be different from and contradictory to those of others. Therefore, if one wishes to recognize even to some extent what this presumed thousand-year kingdom consists of, one must first observe a clear distinction among the Chiliasts. *b)* Some of them make it so crude that they aim for nothing but earthly and fleshly lusts, and this version of their <term>Chiliasm</term> might well be called the crudest of all: such was perhaps that of Cerinthus. Then the Anabaptists did not fail to flatter themselves—during the persecutions they willfully brought upon their own heads—with the hope of a desired golden peace and a kingdom of rest, as can be clearly seen in the examples of Münster, David Joris, and the entire host of Anabaptists. # The Hoped-For Thousand-Year Kingdom

->§. 2.<-

Nothing is more capable of leading our understanding into **prejudices** than the representation of a **pleasant good**. *It is almost so arranged with the characters of most mortals, that they are carried towards joyful things with a more prone credulity than toward gloomy and adverse things.* <note>original Latin: "Est ita fere comparatum cum plerorumque mortalium ingeniis, ut in læta proniore credulitate, quam in tetrica & adversa ferantur."</note> The minds of most people are so constituted that they believe joyful things more readily than those that are adverse and vexatious, as the learned Mr. Heidegger <note>Johann Heinrich Heidegger (1633–1698), a prominent Swiss Reformed theologian known for his work on biblical prophecy</note> writes quite correctly. <margin>i)</margin> The **will** is filled with such violent longing for the good that when a person is told stories of **mountains of gold** <note>a proverbial expression meaning extravagant or impossible promises of wealth</note>, a desire for them immediately arises within him. Especially if he has long not tasted the sweetness of a good suited to his *taste* <note>original German: "gouto," from the French "goût"</note>. And this desire of the will works so violently upon the understanding that it does not rest until it persuades the person to believe that which, if he had enlightened eyes, he would never let himself be persuaded of, nor believe. And since this prejudice offers **hope** specifically regarding a matter that is yet to come, one can understand all the more easily why it finds a place so readily. In this, it remains exactly as **Ludovicus Vives** <note>Juan Luis Vives (1493–1540), a Spanish humanist and scholar</note> once spoke: *There is no matter about which men lie more willingly than about the future, because we hear nothing more willingly, even if we know it is a lie: Thus our favor toward those who boast they can predict the future provokes and nourishes their license.* <note>original Latin: "Nulla res est, de qua libentius homines mentiantur, quam de venturis quoniam nihil nos audimus libentius, etiamfi mentieri sciamus: Ita favor in eos noster, qui futura jactant prædicere, licentiam eorum irritat & alit."</note> There is no matter in which people love untruth more than in things to come; because

### The Character of Weigel’s Writings

it is enough that the writings scattered under his name are full of viper's venom and <term>fanaticism</term> <note>original: *Schwärmerey*. In the 17th and 18th centuries, this was a derogatory term used by orthodox theologians to describe radical mystics who claimed direct inspiration from the Holy Spirit over the written word of the Bible.</note>. Our current inquisitive world sets its heart not so much on Weigel's person, but rather on his writings. These, according to their unjust prejudice, are supposed to be full of spirit and wisdom. These are meant to perfectly reveal and unlock the immeasurable depth of divine mysteries: these are supposed to show the way to heaven much more clearly than the writings of the Prophets and Apostles, and other such unfounded praises.

->§. 2.<-

I consider it unnecessary to investigate at length the origin of this hasty judgment. Since for most people, the very same causes indisputably awaken this high regard that produce such a favorable opinion of other <term>innovators</term> <note>original: *Neulingen*. This refers to those who introduce new, often heterodox, theological ideas.</note>. Rather, I wish to demonstrate that there is not the slightest basis for regarding Weigel's writings as entirely pure, innocent, and moreover as the "core and star, the juice and strength" <note>original: *Kern und Stern, Safft und Krafft*. A rhyming German idiom signifying the absolute essence and vital power of a subject.</note> of **Evangelical Theology**. The devotees of Weigel, after maturely considering what I shall say, will be all the more likely to agree with me if they take to heart that even the godly **Arndt** <note>Johann Arndt (1555–1621), a famous Lutheran theologian. While Arndt's own work *True Christianity* was foundational for Pietism, he was careful to distance himself from the more radical views of Weigel.</note>, who also drew several chapters—though perhaps unknowingly—from this author, nevertheless judged him and his teaching very harshly, and in his unique *Dialogue concerning Christ* <note>original: *Dialogo de Christo* (Latin). This refers to a specific polemical work by Arndt.</note>

In his books on **True Christianity** <note>original: *Christianismo*. This refers to Johann Arndt’s *Vom wahren Christenthum*, one of the most influential works of Protestant piety.</note>, Arndt has shown manifold errors, such as:

1) That he [Weigel] simply rejects the entire **Office of Preaching** <term>Office of Preaching: The formal institution of the church ministry and the public delivery of sermons</term> because of a few "belly-servers" <note>A derogatory term for corrupt clergy who serve their own physical appetites or greed rather than their congregation.</note> and hypocrites. 

2) That he mockingly and scornfully attacks the acceptance of the **Augsburg Confession** <note>The primary confession of faith for the Lutheran Church, presented to Emperor Charles V in 1530.</note>, p. 124. 

3) That he is a terrible slanderer and blasphemer, in whom no gentleness, humility, or friendliness is to be found, but only pure contempt, ibid. 

4) That Christ’s flesh did not come from Adam <note>This refers to a "celestial flesh" Christology, a common heresy among radical reformers who argued Christ’s body was made of heavenly substance rather than human flesh inherited from Adam via Mary.</note>, p. 125. 

5) That Christ must not be reckoned [to us] from the outside <note>original: *zugerechnet*. This attacks the central Lutheran doctrine of "imputed righteousness," where God credits Christ's merit to the believer as a legal standing, rather than an internal transformation.</note>, p. 126. 

6) That we possess the Spirit of God the Father through a direct breathing-in, p. 127. 

7) Likewise, that Christ’s death and merit are not credited to anyone unless he has Christ’s death within himself, p. 128, and so forth. 

I wish from the heart that people would read through these observations deliberately; then they would realize that these are not groundless accusations when Weigel’s writings are accused of such monstrous errors. For surely no **Weigelian** <note>A follower of the mystical and often radical teachings of Valentin Weigel (1533–1588).</note> will easily refuse to look upon and acknowledge **Arndt** as an impartial judge in this matter. However, I wish to demonstrate at greater length that Weigel’s writings are highly dangerous, erroneous, and indeed deviating from Scripture; consequently, they are by no means full of spirit and divine power, but rather lead men into ruin and damnation.

Now, although immediate divine calling <note>A direct, miraculous call from God, such as the Apostles received</note> to the preaching office has ceased today, there nonetheless exists a mediated <note>original: *mittelbahre*; a calling that occurs through established human and church structures</note> calling, where either the whole church or those to whom the church has entrusted this right and office, designate ministers of the Word. And for this reason, Timothy, along with Paul, calls himself a steward of the mystery of **GOD**, even though he was called to it through no immediate vocation <note>original Latin: *Vocation*; a formal call to office</note>, 1 Corinthians 4:1.

Just as the aforementioned writers agree as one, **Jacob Boehme** was born in the year 1575 in Alt-Seydenberg, a village located two miles from Görlitz. His parents did not only send him to school—where, alongside the most important parts of Christianity, he learned to read and write modestly—but initially kept him to the task of herding cattle. After this, he came to Görlitz to learn the shoemaking craft <term>shoemaking craft</term> <note>original: "Schuster-Handwerck"; Boehme is famously known as "The Teutonic Philosopher" and "The Shoemaker of Görlitz."</note>; and once his years of apprenticeship had passed, he set out on his travels <term>journeyman years</term> <note>original: "Wanderschafft"; the traditional period where a craftsman travels to work under different masters before becoming a master himself.</note> in the usual manner.

Because he was by nature of a <term>melancholic complexion</term> <note>According to the medical theory of the four humors, a "melancholic" temperament was associated with earth, black bile, and a tendency toward deep, somber reflection or even depression.</note> and very inclined toward deep brooding—by virtue of which he had already spent his time, whenever he could, poring over the Holy Bible and other books—he continued in this state, creating all sorts of scruples and whims within his mind. It is then said to have happened that a heavenly revelation occurred to him, such that, surrounded by divine light, he stood for seven days in the highest divine contemplation. 

When his years of travel were over, he settled in Görlitz, and after becoming a master, he married Catharina Kuntzschmann, the daughter of a butcher in Görlitz, in the year 1594. In the year 1600, a second enlightenment occurred to him, where he was once again seized by the divine light and, with his <term>starry soul-spirit</term> <note>original: "gestirnten Seelen-Geist"; a term used by Boehme's biographer Abraham von Franckenberg to describe the human spirit's connection to the celestial or "astral" realm.</note> (as Mr. von Franckenberg says), through a sudden glimpse of a pewter...

# Jacob Boehme’s writings

<meta>catchword: My</meta>

vessel, as if by a lovely **Jovial radiance** <term>Jovial radiance</term> <note>original: "Jovialischen Scheins." In Boehme’s mystical system, "Jovial" refers to the planet Jupiter, representing a specific spiritual quality of light, wisdom, and joyful clarity.</note>, he was led into the innermost ground, or the **Center of secret nature**. His third enlightenment is said to have occurred in the year 1610, after which he no longer hesitated to grant his pen the freedom to write; from this, his famous work ***Aurora*** was produced in the year 1612. What lay behind this work was very quickly noticed by the then Head Pastor in Görlitz, **Mr. Gregorius Richter** <note>Richter was a staunch Lutheran traditionalist who viewed Boehme’s mystical claims as dangerous heresy, leading to a lifelong conflict between the two.</note>. For this reason, he petitioned an Honorable Council, asking that Jacob Boehme be compelled in the future to desist from his undertaking. Whereupon Boehme was immediately ordered to abstain from writing books from that time forward.

He lived in obedience to this command for seven whole years; however, after this time, he nevertheless took up the pen anew and composed those writings which now lie in the public light in five **octavo volumes** <term>octavo volumes</term> <note>A book size created by folding a printed sheet three times to form eight leaves.</note>. Finally, he passed away in the year 1624 in Görlitz and was buried in the earth by order of the authorities, accompanied by a funeral sermon. His friends erected an **epitaph** <term>epitaph</term> <note>a commemorative inscription on a tomb or monument.</note> for him, upon which, among other things, this could be read:

->**Born of GOD, died in JESUS, sealed with the Holy Spirit, here rests Jacob Boehme.**<-

However, the grave tablet was broken off again after only a few hours. The funeral inscription, on the other hand, which was composed for him by **Mr. von Ziegler**, consists of the following words:

For no whore or defiled woman can become a virgin, even if she puts on a virgin’s wreath; likewise, no prince, through a pardon, can make her a virgin.* 

25) Item. <note>From the Latin meaning "likewise" or "furthermore."</note> *An imputed righteousness does not count; a stranger cannot inherit God’s kingdom, but rather an **inborn righteousness** from God’s essence,* ibid. <note>Abbreviation for "ibidem," meaning "in the same place" as the previous citation.</note> p. 110. 

Item. *In my very noble talent bestowed upon me by God, I say that one has dipped the cloak of Christ with its purple color into Christ’s blood and taken it as a covering, but with it has only covered the Antichristian child of his own will, and has painted a foreign color onto the Antichristian child of the whore,* p. 138.

## XXII. Prejudice.

### The so-called Labadists possess a correct and incomparably good doctrine.

->§. 1.<-

Whether the Labadists still constitute a public community to this day, and whether many of them still publicly profess this sect <term>sect; in this period, the term "sect" was often used by established church authorities to describe any group that separated from the state-sanctioned church</term>, I cannot say for certain due to a lack of reliable reports. A few years ago, the well-known Mr. Gottfried Arnold <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714) was a famous radical Pietist and church historian whose "Impartial History of the Church and Heretics" defended many groups previously condemned as heretical.</note> is said to have received word that this group is actually still together and continues steadily in their former way of life. <margin>a)</margin> Which I shall leave as it is. However, I can say that I have encountered many in the world who are "Labadist-minded" in their disposition, even if they have never publicly joined such a fanatic group <note>original: "Schwarm," a derogatory term used by the orthodox to describe radical reformers who claimed direct inspiration from the Holy Spirit</note> or entered into an open union with them. Most of those to whom our current Evangelical Church <note>In the 18th-century context, "Evangelical" refers broadly to the Protestant—specifically Lutheran or Reformed—established churches.</note> seems to have fallen into great decay, and who especially wish to appear as if they are urging for a greater holiness of life, exalt de Labadie and his followers as a model and example of genuine Christianity, according to which one should set about a reform of our church

As far as the founder of this sect is concerned, he is the notorious Jean de Labadie <note>Jean de Labadie (1610–1674) was a French mystic and former Jesuit who eventually broke with both the Catholic and Reformed churches to found the communal "Labadist" sect.</note>, the son of a common soldier from Gascony <note>A province in southwestern France.</note>. After Labadie perceived the intention of these people and had already departed from their society, he made the resolution to completely abandon the formerly beloved order in the future and to make a profession of preaching a new Gospel <note>original: "Evangelii"</note>. Scarcely had this become notorious than he was summoned before the Parliament of Bordeaux <note>One of the sovereign high courts of the French judiciary under the old monarchy.</note> to give an account and answer for this. However, he retreated to Geneva, from there to Paris, and finally he went to Amiens in Picardy, where he was appointed by the bishop there as an overseer of the nunneries. But because he did not conduct himself as was fitting for the said bishop, the latter soon dismissed him. we deny with the best right that such was a sufficient light and a salutary guide for even a single Jew who did not see that same light within the light and in the inner illumination of the Spirit. With equal right, we deny that in these times such Holy Scripture—even after being increased by the Books of the Gospel—is sufficient, even for <term>the regenerate</term> <note>Those who have undergone a spiritual rebirth; in this context, the Labadists believe even "born-again" Christians cannot rely on the Bible alone.</note>, to make all actions of true faith and love living without the constant guidance and working of the Holy Spirit. *p)* II.) # and incomparably good teaching.

Words cannot possibly be understood without investigating their meaning and carefully observing the grammatical circumstances; therefore, it is a great rashness to so improperly reject such helpful aids. <note>The "nn)" appears to be a footnote reference or section marker in the original text, likely continuing a list of arguments.</note> *nn)* IV.) It is contrary to the testimony of the Holy Spirit and to daily experience to claim that the recording of the divine Word is an unnecessary work, and that one could well do without it. The Lord Himself says there that His Word was written for the purpose that one might believe, and through such faith be saved (John 20:31). Now, if faith is an absolutely necessary thing, and such a <term>means of salvation</term> <note>original: "Heils-Mittel"</note> without which no one may attain blessedness, how much more necessary must the written version of the divine Word be? This is especially true since one sees daily that, although the clear letter lies before everyone's eyes, nevertheless the lustful curiosity of men always dares to turn the truth into lies. Between the covenant of the Old and New Testaments, there is not the slightest difference such as the Labadists imagine. The former did not consist solely of external letters and ceremonies; rather, through the letter and <term>prototypes</term> <note>The author uses "Vorbilder," referring to "types"—Old Testament events or objects that foreshadow Jesus Christ and the New Covenant.</note> it indicated spiritual and heavenly things. Moses preached not only the Law, but also at the same time—as Paul teaches—the joyful Gospel of the righteousness of faith (Romans 10:6). The sacrifices were also not merely silent ceremonies; rather, one repented for sin through them (Isaiah 1:11, 15; Psalm 51:21). They were simultaneously prototypes of the suffering of Christ; they reconciled and erased, in a certain measure, the sins of humanity (Leviticus 1:4; also Chapter 4:3, 13). The promises of such a covenant were also by no means merely carnal and earthly, but at the same time spiritual and heavenly (Acts 3:15, John 5:39, Romans 4:13).

### Section 7.

Because the power and influence of the **Devil** on earth can be powerfully proven, especially from many examples in **Scripture**, it will be necessary for us to see what **Dr. Bekker** <note>Balthasar Bekker (1634–1698) was a Dutch theologian famous for his book "The World Bewitched," in which he used Cartesian reason to argue that the devil has no physical power or presence in the world.</note> presumes to bring against such examples.
