It does not forbid loving in the slightest; rather, it only wishes to see love directed toward an object worthy of human excellence. If one sets against these arguments those points which are usually put forward to support the "Great Conversion of the Jews," one immediately sees that there is little strength or emphasis to be found in them. I will demonstrate this through a few examples; for my current plan does not allow me to investigate at length all the idle chatter of these unfortunate defenders of the Jews <note>The author refers to "Juden-Vertheidiger" (defenders of the Jews), likely meaning contemporary theologians who held a more optimistic or millenarian view of a future mass conversion.</note>, nor is it worth the effort. Blindness in part has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in; and so all Israel will be saved, as it is written: There shall come out of Zion the Deliverer, and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob.** *Romans 11:25–26.* However, if one only pays a little attention, it will be shown that they do not find in these words what they are looking for. Therefore, Luther <margin>o)</margin> himself previously stated: "Let whoever wants to hope for the whole crowd; I have no hope there, nor do I know of any Scripture for it." <note>This quote reflects Martin Luther's late-life skepticism regarding a mass conversion of the Jewish people, a stance that heavily influenced the author's Lutheran orthodox perspective.</note>

For since the converted Gentiles were now exalting themselves against the Jews and shamefully despising them, the Apostle seeks, with good intentions, to dissuade them from this. And for this purpose, he employs this proof: that God has not rejected each and every Jew, but only a great portion of them because of their persistent <term>hardening</term> <note>Original German: "Verstockung," a theological term for a heart made callous or stubborn against divine grace.</note>. However, if Paul were speaking of a conversion that was only to occur in the future toward the end of the world, he would have acted very imprudently by demanding that the Gentiles cease their habitual contempt for that reason. It would be the same as if someone were to say: "This or that race is rightly to be despised, because many hundreds of years from now, nothing but villains will descend from it." <margin>p)</margin> This text can also be aptly explained in a way that the alleged "Great Conversion of the Jews" is further overturned rather than confirmed. For by <term>μέρος</term> <note>Greek: "meros," meaning "part" or "portion."</note>, a part, the Apostle understands the greatest part of the Jewish people. This latter point is carried by the phrase <term>ἄχρις οὗ</term> <note>Greek: "achris hou," meaning "until" or "so long as."</note>, "so long as." # XXV. Prejudice.

## The punishment of the godless in Hell will surely not last eternally and unceasingly, but they shall one day have a redemption to hope for.

-> §. I. <-

### §. 4.

**II.)** Those testimonies of Scripture in which <term>Election by Grace</term> <note>The theological concept that God chooses specific individuals for salvation.</note> unto eternal life is described as **particular**—meaning that it is not universal like the **General Calling**, but includes only a few—contend against this opinion. This is evident from the words of Jesus when He says: *Many are called, but few are chosen*, Matthew 20:16. If the empty pretense were true—that everyone without exception should be translated into God's eternal Kingdom of Joy after enduring the punishments of hell—then the Savior would have had to say that just as all were called to life, so would they all together become partakers of it; the only difference being that the believers would reach it sooner, while the godless and unbelieving would arrive somewhat later.

### §. 6.

The VIIth ground of proof, which completely destroys this prejudice <note>In this context, "prejudice" refers to the erroneous belief or "preconceived notion" held by some that hell might not be eternal.</note>, is found in Luke 16:26. There, Abraham, standing before God in the blessed life of joy, testifies that between heaven and hell **a great chasm is fixed**, so that one can neither come from the former to the latter, nor from the latter to the former. In these words, it is not only remarkable that the word **is established** <note>original Greek: *ἐστήρικται* (estēriktai)</note> stands there, which indicates an everlasting duration; but Abraham, having been received into the eternal dwellings, also absolutely denies therein that a transition from hell into heaven is possible. For if such a thing were to be hoped for one day, he would have at least indicated it, and referred him <note>Referring to the "Rich Man" in the parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus.</note> to a willing endurance of hellish pain for only some few thousand years.

Matthew 12:31. Which the Evangelist Mark outlines with the following words: 
> Whoever blasphemes the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness forever, but is guilty of eternal judgment. Mark 3:29.

Let no one think that these last words teach, even in the slightest, that some people might expect forgiveness of sins—and by the power of that forgiveness, a release from hell—after death. For it is the custom of Scripture that, in order to represent the absolute impossibility of a thing, it sometimes poses even impossible things as conditional statements. Thus Paul speaks there: 
> Even if we, or an angel from heaven, were to preach a gospel to you other than that which we have preached to you, let him be accursed. Galatians 1:8.

By this, he by no means considers it possible that the angels, who are confirmed in their goodness, could ever become false evangelists; rather, he only wishes to demonstrate that it is impossible to attain salvation through any gospel other than the Apostolic one. Precisely the same sense is found in the passage cited: even if it were possible for sin to be forgiven in that other world <note>Referring to the afterlife or the world to come.</note>, such forgiveness would still not extend to the <term>sin against the Holy Spirit</term> <note>A theological term for "the unpardonable sin," often interpreted as a final, willful rejection of God's grace.</note>. But where there is no forgiveness of sins, there is also no hope for life and salvation. Why then do people struggle so vehemently to argue that eventually all the damned will be torn out of hell?

### §. 8.

I do not wish to cite several more grounds of proof regarding the infinity of the punishment and plague of the damned at this moment; rather, I only wish to remind the reader of this one thing: that if one teaches and believes the opposite, the gate and door to all vices would be thrown wide open. It is true that when the consideration and mental image of eternal hellish punishments is the only thing meant to encourage a person toward virtue, then for the most part, no righteous godliness arises, such as **God** the **Lord** requires from mankind. For **God** wishes to be honored not out of servile fear, but rather out of childlike love. Meanwhile, the reflection upon the infinite torment of hell is nonetheless a powerful sermon of repentance, which shows the sinner what a miserable state he lives in, and what a wretched torture-chamber and room of death he must enter after the conclusion of his wicked life. This consideration then leads the person to earnest repentance for his sin; it provokes and drives him to look for a <term>satisfaction</term> <note>original: "Gnugthuung"; a theological term referring to the atonement or payment for sin that satisfies divine justice.</note> that is valid before **God**; and it is a bridle which still restrains many, so that they do not run with full speed into the desolate, disorderly, and ruinous nature of sin. On the other hand, if a sinner places this prejudice beneath his luxurious lusts like a welcome pillow: *You will not have to remain in hell forever,* then he will not easily from the deep [sleep] of sin—

<header>...shall not [last] forever, etc.</header>

...of which the prophets have spoken; this shows that the **subject** of the **proposition** <note>original: *Subjectum der Proposition*</note> should not be understood generally as all and every thing that **GOD** has created, but rather should only be accepted as those matters proclaimed by the prophets. But where can one find even a single iota expressed concerning either the re-merging <note>original: *Wiedereinfliessung*, literally a "flowing back into"—a mystical concept suggesting that all created beings eventually dissolve back into the divine essence</note> of **creatures** into the divine essence, or the **redemption** of the **damned**? Do not all prophets teach the opposite? For it is written in the prophet **Isaiah**: **Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished, and they shall be an abomination to all flesh, Isa. 66:24.** And in **Daniel**: **Some will arise to eternal shame and disgrace, Dan. 12:2.**

## First Prejudice.

Should **God** then in this day and age no longer make use of immediate revelations <term>Offenbahrungen</term> <note>In this context, "revelations" refers to direct communication from God to individuals, bypasssing traditional church structures.</note> toward mankind; Or should that which has hitherto occurred with the so-called **Inspired ones** <term>Inspirirten</term> <note>The "Inspired" refers to a radical Pietist movement in 18th-century Germany that believed God still spoke through chosen individuals in ecstatic states.</note> and new **Prophets** not be a work of **God**?

### Section V.

I must, however, necessarily begin my treatise with the question of whether there are still **immediate divine inspirations and revelations** today? because the other point concerning the **new prophets** or **Inspired ones** largely depends upon it. Regarding this first question, it is undeniable that a special divine revelation is highly necessary for mankind. There are indeed some natural "sparks" of divine knowledge found within the soul; but they are so small and weak that they provide no sufficient light anywhere, and through their mediation alone, man can nowhere help himself forward; instead, he gropes in darkness, is blind, and knows nothing rightly. The corruption of mankind is also so great that among all nations who have lived without special divine revelations, a powerful abuse of **natural religion** <note>The author refers to "natural religion" as the basic moral and spiritual instincts humans have without the help of the Bible or direct word from God.</note> has emerged. The **heathens** <note>original: "Heyden," referring to non-Christian peoples of antiquity.</note>, who knew nothing of special revelation, not only made cattle into their gods but also truly made their gods into cattle, by attributing such vices to them that were more beastly than human; indeed, they even worshipped the vices themselves as divine, and even made gods out of illnesses, so that one [must marvel] at the blindness and folly...

### §. V.

However, if I recognize Mr. Arnold as the **author** <note>original: *Auctorem*</note> of this work, no one should imagine that I believe everything contained within it comes solely from him. Rather, I am fully convinced that he often served merely as a **channel** through which others—who were perhaps even more ill-disposed toward the **Evangelical Church** <note>In this 18th-century German context, "Evangelical" refers specifically to the Lutheran Church.</note> than he himself—sought to infuse their **deadly poison** into people’s minds. It requires no lengthy evidence to prove this; the matter itself is testimony enough that he must have **plowed with another man’s heifer** <note>original: *mit einem fremden Kalbe müsse gepflüget haben*. This is a biblical idiom from Judges 14:18, meaning to solve a riddle or complete a task by using information or labor belonging to someone else.</note> here and there. 

One only needs to consider the astonishing **erudition** <note>original: *Belesenheit*</note> that shines forth from the work, and the many diverse **original documents** <note>original: *Uhrkunden*</note> cited throughout. How could it be possible for a single person—who was constantly burdened with many other affairs and who also produced a great number of other books—to be capable of gathering so much in such a short time? Every person may believe and hold what they wish regarding this; yet I hope I will be permitted the freedom to believe that Mr. Arnold must have been supported by varied outside assistance. Ultimately, what does it matter to know where such help came from, if only the work itself had not become such a **terrible monstrosity**? <note>original: *Mißgeburth*, literally a "misbirth" or "deformed birth." The author uses this harsh term to describe the book as a theological and historical failure.</note>

### §. VI.

In calling the **History of the Church and Heretics** a terrible **monstrosity** <note>original: *Mißgeburth*. Literally "misbirth," used here to describe the book as a deformed or unnatural creation.</note>, I by no means deny that one or two good things might be found within it. When I encounter something praiseworthy even in the worst **Socinian** <note>Followers of a non-trinitarian movement that denied the divinity of Christ, viewed as a radical heresy by the established church.</note>, **Arminian** <note>Followers of Jacobus Arminius who disagreed with strict Calvinist views on predestination; though less "radical" than Socinians, they were still often viewed with suspicion by the Lutheran orthodox.</note>, and the like, it is my habit to recognize such things as praiseworthy without bias. Why, then, should I not do the same with the writings of such an **author** <note>original: *Auctoris*</note> who, in certain matters, may even deserve some preference over those others? 

Therefore, I do not deny that Mr. Arnold has shown extraordinary diligence in his **Church History**; here and there he has noted several errors in other writers, brought forward many **specific details** <note>original: *Particularia*</note> on various subjects, and so forth. All these circumstances, however, are far from making it an incomparably good or useful book. On the contrary, after conducting a frank and completely impartial examination, I have perceived that the aforementioned work is a very harmful and wicked book, which has caused pure corruption and damage within Christendom. # 68 Arnold’s History of the Church and Heretics

...desired to read it, regardless of whether (according to my previous conception) his theological conscience certainly bound him to do so, he is nonetheless dissatisfied that he has been informed how all teachers of the Church are being so harshly attacked. "I beg you," he wrote, "to consider whether it is consistent with the honor we owe to people whom **God** has placed in office—to whom it also cannot be denied that they performed all sorts of good services for the Church—to make their otherwise unknown faults publicly known for the memory of **posterity**, without any true benefit arising for the common good from it. ## Third Prejudice.

->Without doubt, *Jansenius* and *Quesnel* <note>Cornelius Jansen (1585–1638) and Pasquier Quesnel (1634–1719) were the primary figures of Jansenism, a movement within the Catholic Church that emphasized predestination and divine grace. Their views were condemned by the Papacy in the 17th and 18th centuries, most notably in the bull *Unigenitus*.</note> must possess a very good doctrine, since they are so powerfully attacked by the Pope and his followers, while on the other hand being praised by the Protestants.<-

->§. I.<-

To praise and hold something in high esteem without understanding is indeed a truly foolish thing. Nevertheless, this happens more often than almost anything else. For the majority of people, the situation is not as the Savior speaks: *We speak (and praise) what we know, John 3:11.* <note>original: "Wir reden (und rühmen) das wir wissen, Joh. III, 11." The biblical text (John 3:11) usually reads "We speak what we know," but the author has inserted "and praise" to fit his argument.</note> but rather, *we praise what we imagine to be praiseworthy.* Some need only hear that there is something good to be found in a matter, and the conclusion is already prepared: that such a thing is entirely free from all blameworthy defects. What in truth hardly deserves to be called a faint ray of the breaking dawn must immediately be called a bright, clear day. One sees this clearly in those affairs which have been going on for some time in the Netherlands and France with *Jansenius* and *Quesnel* and their followers. Since in so many writings and accounts about the Roman <note>The text cuts off here. Cornelius Jansenius, a) (who is by no means to be confused with another of the same name, who died as the Bishop of Ghent before this one’s birth and established a special memorial for himself through his *Evangelical Harmony* <note>original: *Harmoniam Evangelicam*; a work harmonizing the four Gospels</note>,) had as his homeland the village of Accoy, located near Leerdam in the Netherlands, where he was born in the year <note>Ao. is an abbreviation for the Latin *Anno*</note> 1585. ### Section III.

We have already mentioned above that a quite extraordinary respect for Augustine was deeply impressed upon Jansenius’s mind. Under this name, countless of the greatest and most learned men in France have sided with *Jansenius’s* party to this very day, and it has been impossible for the Pope to suppress them, even though he has fired all the bolts the Jesuits fashioned against them.

# Jansenius and Quesnel.

In particular, this disposition <note>Referring to the spiritual devotion discussed on the preceding page.</note> was found in a certain *Marquis*, who, out of disgust for the vexatious life at court, intended to spend the remainder of his days in quiet solitude. For this reason, he requested *Quesnel* to provide him with guidance on how he might read the four Evangelists <note>The four Gospels of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.</note> with benefit and edification. The more reasonable this request appeared, the sooner he allowed it to take place, providing him with short moral reflections on every verse of the four Gospels. 

When *Felix Vialard*, Bishop of *Châlons-sur-Marne* p) saw this work, it pleased him to such an extent that, through a circular letter dated November 9, 1671, he recommended it to all the pastors and vicars <note>original: "Vicariis"; assistant priests or representatives of the bishop.</note> of his diocese for diligent reading. He wrote that the author must have studied for a long time in the school of the Holy Spirit to have reached such a great understanding of divine mysteries; he likewise encouraged the creator to continue the work further. 

After *Quesnel* had brought the work to completion over the entire New Testament, it was brought to the public light in the year 1671, though with the concealment of his name. It was received by many with special eagerness, though it was not at all to the taste of the *Jesuits* <note>A powerful Catholic religious order and the primary theological rivals of the Jansenists.</note>. He had also made a very poor name for himself at the Roman Court <note>The Papal administration and its departments.</note> by publishing the works of *Leo the Great* <note>original: "Leonis Magni"; an influential 5th-century Pope.</note>. Because he had, at most, disapproved of the proceedings of **Leo the Great** <note>original: "Leonis M." (Leonis Magni)</note> against **Hilary** <note>Hilary of Arles, a 5th-century bishop who clashed with the papacy over jurisdictional rights.</note>, and had thus stepped a bit too close to **Papal Infallibility**, the aforementioned edition was soon forbidden and condemned by the Pope. After this, the **Jesuits** began anew to once again persecute the admirers and followers of **Jansenius** and to destroy the peace established in this regard by **Clement IX**. The Archbishop of Paris, **de Harlay** <note>François de Harlay de Champvallon, known for his strict enforcement of anti-Jansenist policies.</note>, went so far as to demand that all teachers and clergy swear the former oath against Jansenius and his condemned propositions. Most accommodated themselves; **Quesnel**, however, to avoid this, went to Orléans, and from there he fled—out of fear of greater trouble—to Brussels, where he also encountered the old, honest **Arnauld** <note>Antoine Arnauld, a leading Jansenist philosopher and theologian.</note>. Both were then ordered to vacate this place as well; they therefore turned toward Leiden, Rotterdam, and Liège, but finally they returned secretly to Brussels, where Quesnel lived in total hiding. q) However, as the persecution of the **Jansenists** rose ever higher, and Quesnel was accused of having misled others, the Archbishop of **Mechelen** <note>A city in present-day Belgium, also known as Malines.</note> had him taken into custody in the year 1703. Doubtless he would have had very little reward to hope for if he had not, through the mediation of good friends, broken through a wall and escaped the imminent evil

### §. V.

Regarding the conduct of the **Roman Pope** and the other enemies of **Jansenism** <note>A theological movement within Catholicism emphasizing original sin and divine grace, often opposed by the Jesuits.</note> against this famous man and his **New Testament** <note>Paschasius Quesnel’s most famous work, "The New Testament in French with Moral Reflections," which became a flashpoint for religious conflict.</note>, it is unbelievable how strict and harsh it was. In the year 1710, at the instigation of the embittered **Jesuits**, the bishops of **La Rochelle** and **Luçon** had a mandate posted on every corner of the city of **Paris**, even on the **Archbishop’s Palace**, in which they exhorted and warned all Catholic Christians to guard themselves most carefully against Father Quesnel’s seductive book, lest they draw poison and death from it. Furthermore, the Archbishop, **Cardinal de Noailles** <note>Louis Antoine de Noailles, the Archbishop of Paris who initially approved Quesnel’s book, leading to a long-standing conflict with the Crown and Rome.</note>, was accused of being a particular support for Quesnel and of seeking to promote Jansenism. The Jesuits blackened both their names so much before the King <note>Louis XIV of France.</note> that the matter—without any consideration for the **French Church Liberties** <note>Also known as the Gallican Liberties, which asserted that the French King and Church had certain rights independent of the Pope's authority.</note>—immediately reached the Roman Pope. The latter arranged an assembly of several Jesuit-minded Cardinals, who [judged] Quesnel’s...

They should examine the New Testament according to the rule of the Catholic faith. In a word, the conclusion was reached before the examination had even properly begun, and on September 8, 1713, the famous Constitution called *Unigenitus* <note>A Papal Bull issued by Pope Clement XI. Its name comes from the opening Latin words "Unigenitus Dei Filius" (The Only-Begotten Son of God).</note> was finally issued, in which 101 propositions drawn from Quesnel’s New Testament were most emphatically condemned. During the lifetime of the previous King <note>Louis XIV of France, who supported the Pope's decree to ensure religious unity in his kingdom.</note>, fear forced many to accept this Bull in blind obedience against their better knowledge and conscience; but after his death, one after another stood their ground again <note>The original German idiom "auf die Hinterbeine getreten" literally means "stepped on their hind legs," like a horse rearing up in resistance.</note>, and since then, one has heard of nothing in France but revocations and appeals to a "better-informed Pope" <note>A legal maneuver where the clergy appealed the Pope's decision to a future General Council of the Church or to a Pope who was better advised on the facts.</note>.

### §. VI.

If one were to ask me now whether I, along with many thousands of others, do not also disapprove of the Pope’s proceedings against both Jansenius and Quesnel; I cannot deny that I find much good in both writings, even in the condemned propositions themselves, and must therefore confess that, by right, the Pope should have shown himself differently, as a better lover of the truth. Among the rejected propositions of Jansenius <note>Cornelius Jansenius (1585–1638), the theologian whose work "Augustinus" founded the Jansenist movement.</note>, the most prominent is this: "Some of God's commandments are impossible for just men who wish and strive to follow them according to the present strength they have; they also lack the grace by which they might become possible." <note>original: "Aliqua Dei præcepta hominibus justis volentibus & conantibus secundum præsentes, quas habent vires, sunt impossibilia; deest illis quoque gratia, qua possibilia fiant"</note> Some of God’s commandments are, even for the righteous and those people eager to live according to them, [impossible] according to their... <meta>The sentence continues on the following page with "ren" (ihren/their).</meta>

### §. VII.

But the **New Testament of Father Quesnel** <note>Pasquier Quesnel (1634–1719), a French Oratorian priest whose Jansenist-leaning commentary on the New Testament became a flashpoint for religious conflict.</note>, which was rejected and condemned by the Pope, seems to be filled with an even greater knowledge of the truth. In particular, the **system of ethics** <term>moral theology|Morale</term> which he emphasizes throughout is quite beautiful and exceptional in many respects, especially as it is presented in a lively, moving, and pleasant writing style. The 101 propositions which the Pope had extracted from it and condemned in his famous **Bull** <note>The Papal Bull *Unigenitus Dei Filius* (1713) issued by Pope Clement XI, which condemned 101 specific sentences from Quesnel’s work as heretical.</note> have the reputation—not only among Quesnel’s friends but also among many Protestants—of being entirely consistent with Holy Scripture and the sayings of the early Church Fathers. It is not necessary to demonstrate this with many examples, because entire writings on the subject are plainly available to the public.

# Polygamy and Keeping Concubines #

<margin>
a) I have here summarized the words of the defenders of simultaneous marriage... <note>The margin note is partially cut off in the source but refers to the author's method of presenting the opposition's arguments for the sake of debate.</note>
</margin>

[...de]sires, and seeks to excuse his untamed immoderation in the following way: One can surely take more than one wife, if only one can support them, or one may keep a **concubine** <note>original: *Concubine*; a woman who lives with a man in a marriage-like relationship but without the legal or social status of a wife.</note> alongside his regular spouse, with whom he also begets children, even if he does not **treat** <note>original: *tractiret*.</note> her equally to his regular wife in all respects, nor allows her children to enjoy all the same **privileges**, rights, and advantages as the other children. Why should that be a sin? Where has God ever forbidden it? Where is it written in the Ten Commandments: "You shall not have more than one wife in marriage"? I know well that **fornication** <note>original: *Hurerey*.</note> and adultery are forbidden, and I certainly consider both to be grave sins. But how could it be a sin if, precisely for the purpose of avoiding fornication and adultery, I wish to take more than one wife—not that I seek only to satisfy my lust with her, but rather that I may beget children with her? I also concede that the authorities, for certain reasons, may forbid public and generally practiced **polygamy** or **concubinage**, for many a man is hardly **capable** of supporting his one and only wife and the children he has begotten with her. What a burden would **society** face if he were to take even more wives and only weigh down the community with a great multitude of children whom he himself cannot provide for, and who consequently trouble others with begging?

...let a woman have her own husband. If one compares this with other ways of speaking, one will see what the true understanding of it is. <term>For example</term> <note>original: "Z. E." (Zum Exempel)</note>: For the sake of order, let every city have its council, and let every council have its own city. <term>Likewise</term> <note>original: "It." (Item)</note>: Let every lord have his chamberlain, and let every chamberlain have his own lord. Let every merchant have his own shop <note>original: "Gewölbe"; literally a "vault," but historically referring to a merchant's arched shop or storeroom.</note>, and every shop have its own merchant, <term>etc.</term> <margin>o) <note>original Latin: "Ipse Cicero Epist. 7. ad Famil. Thus, it is in vain to point out that the word <term>idios</term> <note>Greek for "one's own," "private," or "peculiar."</note> does not always exclude plurality. I concede this point, but it cannot be applied here, because the phrasing and the entire context do not permit it. Therefore, whenever such an excuse is brought forward, one should simply take the words as a whole—and indeed, both parts of the sentence together—and imagine another example in the same form; then the inadequacy of such excuses will be recognized by itself. 

In short: what is "own" is indivisible and does not allow for sharing <note>original: "Gemeinschafft"; the state of being held in common.</note>, otherwise it would be *common* and not *own*. Now, if a woman is to have her own husband, and have the sole right to the same, then it remains true that the number "two" admits no "third" here, and that the taking of many wives is contrary and opposed to **God’s** order. On this, the profoundly learned **Dr. Dann-** <meta>hauer</meta> writes very well...

senses are to be found. **God** has indeed said: *Be fruitful and multiply!* <note>original German: "Seyd fruchtbar und mehret euch!" referencing Genesis 1:28.</note> But He certainly did not mean this simply without any order, as if man should only see to it that he fills society with a great multitude of children. When **God** speaks to people: *Be fruitful and multiply!* He intends that humans should multiply *as humans*. This command is to be understood no differently than when **God** says: *You shall eat the herbs*—that is, everything that the earth brings forth. It does not follow from this that **God** wants man to do nothing but eat and stuff his body full; rather, this is to be understood within its proper order and with regard to its purpose, namely that man should eat only as much as is useful for his preservation. The same applies to this command: *Multiply*, namely, as much as is necessary for the preservation of the human race. When **God** says: *Be fruitful and multiply!* He does not want people merely to mingle with one another and bring many children into the world; rather, His intention is that parents should fill the world with such children who also live as rational human beings, learn something useful, perform useful services for human society, and make their way through the world honestly. # Polygamy and Keeping a Concubine

The scandal would be unbearable, but the Landgrave <note>Philip I, Landgrave of Hesse (1504–1567), a leading champion of the Reformation who caused a crisis by marrying a second wife while still married to his first.</note> should be satisfied that he can keep his mistress <note>original: "Metze," a term used at the time for a concubine or mistress.</note> secretly with a good conscience, according to His Princely Grace’s own report and the advice of his Confessional Council. Furthermore, when they referred in their deliberation to Luther’s sermons on **Genesis 16** <note>This chapter of the Bible describes Abraham taking Hagar as a second wife because Sarah was barren.</note>, in which Luther had written that the patriarchs had not sinned when they took two wives—indeed, that he could not forbid it even today, though he would not advise it—he answered as follows: he had frequently taught that one must not reintroduce the Law of Moses, although in a case of necessity one could make use of it secretly, or even publicly if the civil authority commanded it. He added that the examples of others are of no use, for it does not follow that what one person does out of necessity, another has the right to do. One might well steal bread without punishment in a case of extreme hunger and need, but for that reason, it is not permitted to everyone. For the rest, he advises the Landgrave to keep the matter secret and to have the ministers in his lands preach earnestly against **polygamy**; and he concludes, finally, that he could defend the Landgrave’s case **before God** because of the private confession, but **before the world** and according to common law, he neither could nor would defend it.

Finally, we consider **Ambrose** in *Book I on Father Abraham, Chapter IV*, where he excuses **Abraham**—who joined himself to **Hagar** during the lifetime of his wife **Sarah**—by saying: "Abraham existed before the Law of Moses and before the Gospel, and therefore adultery was not yet forbidden" <note>original Latin: "Abrahamum ante legem Mosis & ante Evangelium extitisse, adeoque nondum interdictum fuisse adulterium;"</note>; that is: because Abraham lived before the Law of Moses and before the Gospel, it seems that adultery was not yet forbidden at that time. This must certainly be counted among the *blemishes of Ambrose* <term>Naevos Ambrosii: a Latin phrase used by later scholars to denote the theological errors or "spots" found in the writings of Saint Ambrose</term>, for as the saying goes: "Even great men may err!"

Thus, the **opponents** can provide no solid **reason** for **polygamy** <term>Polygamy: the practice of having more than one spouse at the same time</term> and **concubinage** <term>Concubinage: a domestic relationship similar to marriage but without the legal status of a full marriage</term>. # The Fifth Prejudice.
## That Man, in His Natural State, Still Possesses Great and Extraordinary Powers of the Soul.

### Section 1.

This preconceived opinion is certainly found among far more people than one would hardly suspect. When one asks those who profess their faith in the Evangelical Church <note>In this 18th-century context, "Evangelical" (Evangelische Kirche) refers specifically to the Lutheran Church.</note> what they hold concerning the Fall of the first humans and the original sin <term>original sin (Erbsünde): the Christian doctrine that humanity exists in a state of sin and alienation from God as a result of Adam's fall.</term> descending therefrom, most indeed give such an answer that would lead one to think they regard the human soul as a being entirely stripped of the powers bestowed by God, and become completely incapable of any good. However, if one pays closer attention to their behavior, one is quite easily convinced that, in this matter, their heart must harbor a far different opinion than what they profess with their mouth. For they betray, in both worldly and spiritual actions, that they attribute far too much to their natural powers and imagine them to be much more perfect than they are in reality. How many do not imagine that their understanding is so sharp-sighted that it is not subject to the slightest danger of any error in the recognition <note>original: "Erkänntniß"</note> and judgment of natural truths. Should they, for the general

If they are entangled in all sorts of adversities, they believe they will be most easily liberated from them if they take counsel from their own understanding, and they think no further of divine help or assistance. If they wish to undertake something important, how little do they concern themselves with partaking in a heavenly blessing; how, on the other hand, do they trust and build upon their own strength, art, and dexterity? If they encounter all sorts of sorrowful and adverse events, then their **mere reason** must serve as a source of comfort; they gather together all the arguments by which they wish to provide themselves relief from their pain, and they are of the mind that if one only follows the rules of one's reason in a fitting manner, then no misery is so intense or great that one could not display a bold composure. <note>The original term here is *Gelassenheit*, a significant concept in German theology implying a state of calm, yielded equanimity, though here the author critiques it as a product of "mere reason" rather than faith.</note>

In spiritual matters, it happens much the same way. Many read the most holy Word of God without any enlightenment prayed for from on high; and nevertheless, they hope to gain a precise and correct understanding of it. Many go to church without the slightest preparation; and nevertheless, they imagine they are hearing, understanding, and applying the divine word in a salvific <term>salvific (heilsamlich): leading to or intended for spiritual salvation.</term> way. Many occasionally even form the resolution to begin a virtuous life—

One wants to live quite rationally; one wants to free one’s understanding from all prejudices; one wants to most carefully avoid the opportunity for all sinful conduct; one wants to moderate, tame, or even completely root out the affections <note>original: *Affecten*—in this period, this referred to strong emotions or passions that were thought to overwhelm reason.</note>, or movements of the mind, according to the prescription of reason. In such a way, one indeed imagines the powers of the soul in their natural state to be very great and perfect, and attributes to them such effects as can be successfully completed in no other way than through the assistance of the Spirit of God. Most of all, however, one sees those afflicted with such a harmful error who, above others, wish to possess an enlightened, capable, sharp-sighted, and penetrating understanding. Among such people, the still-remaining natural strength must do everything; God’s grace and the working of the Holy Spirit come into no particular <term>consideration (Consideration): meaning here to be taken into account or given weight in one's planning.</term>

Even if they might still say with their mouths that through the wretched Fall into Sin, the human soul has been greatly enfeebled and weakened, they nevertheless say, because of their supposed laudable and good deeds: "My hands and the strength of my hands have the power to accomplish this," and in doing so they do not think of the Lord their God, who [gives them the power to do so.] <note>The sentence ends abruptly here, as is common with catchwords; it continues on the following page.</note>

### §. II.

However, in all times, people have been found in great numbers who have excessively elevated natural powers and derived from them such effects for which a communicated divine power is necessarily required. The pagans <note>original: *Heyden*—referring here to the ancient Greeks and Romans.</note> at least believed this much: that without the powerful cooperation, providence, and blessing of their supposed gods, their crops, their households, etc., could not thrive or grow successfully. But as far as the proper conduct of life, the practice of virtue, the attainment of a blessed state after death, and so forth were concerned, they considered the soul’s own powers to be entirely sufficient. For this reason, they sent no prayers or sighs <note>original: *Seuffzer*—in this context, brief, heartfelt internal prayers or aspirations directed toward God.</note> to their gods, but thought they could live virtuously enough on their own. # The Sixth Prejudice.

## Sunday is not instituted by God, and Christians are not necessarily bound to Sunday.

### §. I.

Just as highly as the benefit of God is esteemed by righteous Christians—in that the holy Sunday is given to them as a day of rest for their souls and for their spiritual edification—so despicably is this day despised by the <term>children of the world (Weltkinder)<gloss>a term used in Pietist literature to describe people focused on secular pleasures and material life rather than spiritual devotion</gloss></term>. These people are accustomed to saying of the feast days, just as those mockers in the Old Testament once did:
> Why must one day be holier than another? Since the sun makes all days in the year the same.

Sirach 33:7. <note>The author cites the Book of Sirach (also known as Ecclesiasticus), a book of the Apocrypha. The verse argues that God distinguished days and seasons despite them all being made by the same sun.</note> No day in the whole week is spent by people with more extravagance than this day, which was so singularly distinguished by God. If one were to ask a child of the world what Sunday is, one could take no other description from their entire conduct than this: Sunday is a day on which one can pursue one pleasurable delight after another, go into the taverns, and there dance, jump, drink, and gorge themselves. As all Christians are now bound to this...

Now, just as the word **Sabbath** according to its origin means nothing other than a **Day of Rest**: so, through the usage of holy Scripture, it is commonly understood to mean the seventh day of the week; and this is again taken in two ways. It either signifies generally such a day sanctified for the service of God, which is selected out of the seven days of the week; or it signifies in particular that day of rest which falls *precisely* and *specifically* <note>original: "præcise und determinate"</note> on the last day of the week, or on our so-called **Saturday**. This latter is also called the **Jewish Sabbath**, *c)* because it was prescribed to the Jewish people by Moses at God’s command, and had to be celebrated in a strict manner, with abstention from all work, even the slightest, according to the constitution of the **Ceremonial Law**. The former, however, may very fittingly be called the **Creation-Sabbath**, because it was instituted by God and ordered to be celebrated immediately after the Creation. God, therefore, wished the Sabbath to be known as sanctified because He had sanctified it with His own rest from the works of creation. Now, however, this is a universal cause that concerns all mankind. For all people are bound to contemplate and honor God as the Creator of heaven and earth; therefore, all people are obligated to celebrate the seventh day, because God desires that the works of creation be contemplated on that very day. ## §. X.

Furthermore, it is argued that worship in the *New Testament* is bound to no time nor place, but rather must be performed by Christians at all times. For example, on his birthday, where he must join with *David* in singing:

> I thank thee for this, that I am wonderfully made! Wonderful are all thy works, and that my soul knows well, *Ps. 139:14.*

### §. XIII.

From this it is now clearly evident that every upright Christian is still bound today to the God-hallowed celebration of Sunday. I only add the following remarks. "To the law and to the testimony!" says the Lord; "if they do not speak according to this word, they have no dawn," Isaiah 8:20. And as many as walk according to this rule and infallible guideline, peace and mercy be upon them, Galatians 6:16. Hence, it is rightly said even in Canon Law <term>Jure Canonico</term> c): <note>original Latin: "Eos condemnamus, qui se extollunt adversus Scripturas"</note> "We condemn all those who exalt themselves against the Scriptures."

### ->§. IX.<-

II) Simple faith among the lowly and unrefined people is indeed good and wholesome, but it is not, for that reason, the very best faith. We cannot deny this much: that if an ordinary Christian has correctly recognized the most necessary parts of Christian doctrine and places his trust upon them with his whole heart, he thereby obtains justification before **GOD** in this time of grace, and eternal salvation after death. For there are various degrees and stages of knowledge, just as there are of other spiritual gifts; and the fact that such knowledge is found more perfectly in one person than in another in no way negates the essence of faith. Although even the lowly and the very simplest people are obligated to broaden and increase their knowledge, **GOD** nevertheless does not count it toward eternal damnation that they have, so to speak, remained standing on the first or second step of knowledge—provided that they have had no opportunity, means, or ability to climb ever higher. By right, even the least among the people, once he has grasped the most necessary fundamental doctrines, should thereafter be mindful to grow and increase in the knowledge of **GOD** from day to day. For many, however—indeed, for most—this is entirely impossible. For to begin with, one might well say what the Chamberlain <note>The "Chamberlain" refers to the Ethiopian Eunuch in Acts 8:31, who, when asked if he understood the scriptures, replied, "How can I, except some man should guide me?"</note> said of himself: They have no one to guide them,

they cannot deduce one thing from another, and so forth.

little of Christian doctrine beyond what is

## The *Eukleria* of Schurman <note>original Greek: εὐκληρία; the title of Schurman’s spiritual autobiography, meaning "choosing the better part" or "well-allotted portion."</note>
<meta>catchword: hear</meta>

...perpetual fame, that although she possessed extraordinary learning, art, and skill, she nevertheless allowed a special modesty and humility to shine through in all her letters and writings. If many a person had only a tenth part of her knowledge, he would perhaps boast and strut with it more than she was accustomed to do, despite possessing such a great wealth of intellectual gifts.

->§. V.<-

It is most regrettable that this praiseworthy person, as she advanced in age, fell among the **Labadist pack of fanatics** <term>Labbadistische Schwärmer-Rotte</term> <note>The Labadists were a 17th-century radical Pietist communal sect led by Jean de Labadie. The author uses the derogatory term "Rotte" (pack/gang) and "Schwärmer" (fanatics) to express orthodox disapproval of their mystical and separatist views.</note>, as has already been mentioned. For then she began to reject all worldly sciences and to approve of nothing but the extravagant dreams of her **lying prophet** <note>A reference to Jean de Labadie (1610–1674), the leader of the sect, whom the author considers a false teacher.</note>, as can be sufficiently gathered from her book titled <term>Eukleria</term> <note>εὐκληρία</note>. The first part of this work was published during her lifetime at Altona in 1673; the other part, however, did not come to the light of public day until after her fatal passing in 1684 at Amsterdam. It is doubted by some, not without reason, whether it is an authentic child of its alleged mother <note>The author is questioning the authenticity of the second volume of *Eukleria*, suggesting it may have been edited or written by others after Schurman's death.</note>. For just as today's lustful world loves forbidden fruit the most, there is no lack of curious and ill-behaved minds who claim that this <term>Eukleria</term> <note>original Greek: Εὐκληρία, meaning "the better choice" or "well-allotted portion." ### §. XI.

The 5th, 6th, 7th, and eighth chapters contain a description of the **Labadist community** <note>The Labadists were a 17th-century community of Dutch Pietists founded by Jean de Labadie. Therefore, the great teacher Gregory <note>Pope Gregory I (c. 540–604), known as Gregory the Great, a foundational theologian for both the Catholic and Protestant traditions.</note> writes very profoundly: *True faith is that which does not contradict in its conduct what it says in words; For then we are truly faithful, if we fulfill in works what we promise in words* <note>original Latin: "Vera fides est, quæ in hoc, quod verbis dicit, moribus non contradicit; Tunc enim veraciter fideles sumus, si quod verbis promittimus, operibus complemus;"</note>. He means that faith and a virtuous life must be inseparably united with one another.

### §. X.

The seventh **Article** contains, along with various others, this primary error: that a person in this mortal life could reach a point where they commit no more sin at all.

> "All," it says, "in whom **Christ** has taken shape through the **new creation** <term>neue Creatur: A biblical concept of spiritual renewal or rebirth in the believer.</term>, or who are born of **God**, bear this mark: that they no longer sin, but keep themselves from the Evil One, even though they are still incited and tempted by the **serpent’s seed** <note>original: *Schlangen-Saamen*; a reference to the lingering presence of original sin or worldly corruption.</note> that still lives in their flesh." p. 433.

To refute this proposition, and to avoid being overly long-winded, I refer to what has been cited elsewhere regarding it. However, the holy **Lord's Prayer** <term>Vater Unser: The prayer Jesus taught his disciples, used here as a theological argument.</term> shows its falsehood very clearly. Without doubt, the disciples of **Jesus** must be regarded as the kind of people who were born of **God** and in whom **Jesus** had taken shape. Even assuming they had not yet reached that state when they petitioned their Master for a **form of prayer** <note>original: *Gebeths-Formul*</note>, they unquestionably became so afterward. Nevertheless, the **Lord** prescribes that they, among other things, also pray for the **forgiveness of sins**, Luke 11:4. This is proof enough that they, despite their spiritual **rebirth** <term>Wiedergeburth: The Pietist emphasis on a radical, internal transformation of the believer.</term>, must still have had sin within them; otherwise, they would not have been permitted to ask for its remission. Just as the bright sun has its **spots** <note>original: *Maculas*; Latin for spots, often used in this period to refer to sunspots.</note> and stains, so too do even the most—

Aa 4

...absurd. The Holy Supper is not food with which I am to satisfy a hungry stomach, but rather one in which I am to receive the body and blood of Christ. Tell me, however, whether this cannot happen in a small *dose* <note>original: *Dosi*, a Latin-inflected form of dose</note> just as well and truly as in a large one. That the laity <term>laity: the "ordinary" members of the church congregation, as opposed to the ordained clergy</term> behave reverently when receiving the Holy Supper certainly deserves praise, because it is an awe-inspiring mystery, toward which one can never show as much reverence as one has cause to do. 

And what is so reprehensible about being hushed <note>original: *maußstille*, literally "mouse-still," meaning perfectly silent or still</note> during the enjoyment of the Holy Supper? And so that it is not necessary to go through each one: He who gave it to Constantine the Christian, gave it also to the apostate Julian.** <note>original Latin: "Deus dat felicitatem in regno cœlorum solis piis: Regnum vero terrenum & piis, sicut ei placet... qui Constantino Christiano, ipse apostatæ Juliano"</note> God grants happiness in the kingdom of glory only to the pious. However, the earthly world-kingdom He gives to the good as well as the evil, according to what pleases Him; now, nothing unjust pleases Him. Thus, He who shared dominion with Marius, also did so with Caius Caesar; He who gave it to Augustus, gave it also to Nero; He who gave it to both Vespasians, Father and Son, as praiseworthy Emperors, also gave it to the cruel tyrant Domitian. And so that we do not mention each and every one, He who bestowed the government upon the Christian Emperor Constantine, also gave it to the apostate Julian. ## §. IV.

We add, fifthly (V), as an irrefutable testimony of their wicked and malicious disposition, the dreadful blasphemies, insults, and mockery which the Jews audaciously pour out against the Holy One of **GOD**, against the true **Messiah JESUS** of **Nazareth**, against the Christian religion, against the books of the **New Testament**, and against everything that has a **connection** <note>original: "Connexion"</note> and relationship to them. ## §. IX.

It is furthermore claimed: Even if the **Jews** did not believe in **JESUS** of **Nazareth** as the true **Messiah** <term>Messiah: derived from the Hebrew word for "Anointed One," referring to the promised savior of the Jewish people</term>, they nevertheless believed in the **Messiah** in general, and this could in no way hinder their **salvation** <note>original: "Seligkeit" — refers to eternal state of grace or being "blessed" in heaven</note>, even if they were mistaken about the specific person. However:
I) There is a great difference between the times before the arrival and revelation of the **Messiah**, and the times after it. Before his arrival, it was sufficient that the **Israelites** only hoped generally for the universal Savior of the world, even if they did not know him precisely in every detail and circumstance. For **GOD** had not yet revealed everything to them so exactly and clearly. ### §. X.

It is also claimed that Christ has made **satisfaction** <term>satisfaction (Gnugthuung) — the theological doctrine that Christ’s suffering and death paid the debt of human sin to satisfy divine justice</term> for all people, and that he has reconciled the entire world with **GOD**. Therefore, it is argued that the Jews could also be justified and saved before **God** in view of the satisfaction provided for all people, if they only held to **God** with simple hearts and were ready to believe and do everything that **God** demanded of them. It is suggested that it is not necessary to recognize and embrace Christ's satisfaction so very precisely and clearly; rather, **God** attributes it to all those who do not resist the workings of the **Holy Spirit**. Now, the **Holy Spirit** could indeed work among the Jews if He were to drive their hearts toward true fear of God, truth, and righteousness.

To this, the following serves as an answer: that the satisfaction and redemption of **Jesus Christ** is indeed universal and concerns all people in terms of its **acquisition** <note>This refers to "meriting" salvation—the idea that Christ's death was sufficient to pay for every person's sins</note>; however, for the actual **communication** <note>The process by which the benefits of Christ's death are actually applied to an individual</note> and enjoyment of this salvation, a certain order has been prescribed by **God**. To this order belongs the requirement that a person must allow the Spirit of **GOD**, who testifies of Christ, to work within them. He testifies of Christ through the word of the *Gospel* <note>original: "Evangelii"</note>, and through the preaching of the same, He awakens in the person true saving faith, *Romans 10, verse 14*: **How then shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard?** Furthermore, the satisfaction of Christ benefits no one except those who [believe] in him—
